title: English with Kyle
topic: Countable/Uncountable with Any/Some · The More...The Less · It Depends On · Phrasal Verbs with Put · To Have Trouble + -ing

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Hay tigres en Rusia. | Are there any tigers in Russia? |
| Hay correo para mí. | Is there any mail for me? |
| No ha habido incendios forestales este verano. | There haven't been any forest fires this summer. |
| No me des agua. | Don't give me any water. |
| Necesito sal. | I need some salt. |
| Por muy sincero que seas, él no te creerá. | No matter how sincere you are, he won't believe you. |
| Cuanto menos vayas allí, mejor para todos. | The less you go there, the better for everyone. |
| Cuanto más trabajo, menos eficaz soy. | The more I work, the less effective I am. |
| Cuanto más escuches, más aprendes. | The more you listen, the more you'll learn. |

**Key notes:**

- **any** goes in questions and negatives (to ask about or deny existence): *Are there **any** tigers in Russia? Don't give me **any** water.* **some** goes in affirmative statements: *I need **some** salt.*
- Avoiding the double negative: you can't say ~~there isn't no~~ — say *there isn't **any** water.*
- **No matter how + adjective + subject + verb** = *por muy + adjetivo + que + subjuntivo*: *No matter how sincere you are, he won't believe you.*
- **The + comparative…, the + comparative…** (double comparative): *The less you go there, the better. The more I work, the less effective I am. The more you listen, the more you'll learn.*
- **less** (uncountable — an amount, e.g. of time) vs. **fewer** (countable — a number of occasions): *the less you go there* refers to the amount of time spent, so *less* is correct here rather than *fewer*.

sections.title: 2. It Depends On
sections.content:
**Structure:** *it depends on* — always with the **-s** (never ~~it depend~~), always followed by **on** (never ~~depends of~~ or ~~it's depend~~), and treated como si fuera una sola palabra — a fixed chunk you can drop into almost any sentence.

> *Depende del tiempo.* → **It depends on** the weather.

### It Depends On — Drill

items.text: It depends on you.
items.speak: It depends on you.

items.text: It depends on me.
items.speak: It depends on me.

items.text: It depends on the weather.
items.speak: It depends on the weather.

items.text: It depends on who you ask.
items.speak: It depends on who you ask.
items.secondary: Depende de a quién le preguntes.

items.text: It depends on my mother.
items.speak: It depends on my mother.

items.text: It depends on a lot of factors.
items.speak: It depends on a lot of factors.

items.text: It depends on how you go.
items.speak: It depends on how you go.

items.text: It depends on the budget.
items.speak: It depends on the budget.

audio_blocks.content_after:
**Notes:**

- Connected speech: *it* + *depends* links — the final **t** of *it* connects into the **d** of *depends* ("i-de-pends").
- Short form: *Well, that depends* — *Bueno, eso depende* — the -s still never drops, it just omits the *on + noun*.

sections.title: 3. Phrasal Verbs with 'Put' (Review)
sections.content:
Kyle revisited this set of phrasal verbs built on **to put** — same base verb, different meaning depending on the particle (first covered in the [Jul 7 class](/?class=kyle_20260707)).

| Phrasal verb | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **put out** | to extinguish (a fire or flame) |
| **put on** | to dress yourself / wear a specific item |
| **put in / put into** | to insert |
| **put up** | to place something where it's normally kept, or somewhere elevated |
| **put away** | to store something in its place |
| **put off** | to postpone / procrastinate |
| **put up with** | to tolerate — *aguantar, soportar* (almost always negative) |
| **put back** | to return something to its original place |

### Put — Drill

items.text: I put out the candle with my fingers.
items.speak: I put out the candle with my fingers.

items.text: You put on a sweater before you go outside.
items.speak: You put on a sweater before you go outside.

items.text: Put the coin in the slot.
items.speak: Put the coin in the slot.

items.text: They put up the flag every morning.
items.speak: They put up the flag every morning.

items.text: I put away my gardening tools because it was going to rain.
items.speak: I put away my gardening tools because it was going to rain.

items.text: The match was put off due to the rain.
items.speak: The match was put off due to the rain.

items.text: I can't put up with the noise.
items.speak: I can't put up with the noise.

items.text: Please put it back where you found it.
items.speak: Please put it back where you found it.

audio_blocks.content_after:
**Related:** *can't stand* is another way to say *can't put up with*, and — like *put up with* — is almost always used in the negative: *I can't stand that noise.*

**Bonus idiom:** *something is **growing on** me* = you're starting to like it more over time (not a "put" phrasal verb, but came up in the same conversation): *Tomatoes are starting to grow on me.*

sections.title: 4. To Have Trouble + -ing
sections.content:
**Structure:** *have trouble* + **-ing** = *costar trabajo / tener dificultad para*

> *Me cuesta trabajo entenderte.* → I have trouble understanding you.

### To Have Trouble — Drill

items.text: I have trouble understanding you.
items.speak: I have trouble understanding you.

items.text: Do you have trouble getting up in the morning?
items.speak: Do you have trouble getting up in the morning?
items.secondary: ¿Te cuesta trabajo levantarte por la mañana?

items.text: Did you have trouble getting used to Spanish food?
items.speak: Did you have trouble getting used to Spanish food?
items.secondary: ¿Te costó trabajo acostumbrarte a la comida española?

items.text: I have trouble remembering all my passwords.
items.speak: I have trouble remembering all my passwords.
items.secondary: Tengo problemas para recordar todas mis contraseñas.

items.text: I have trouble sleeping at night.
items.speak: I have trouble sleeping at night.
items.secondary: Tengo problemas para dormir por la noche.

items.text: Does your boss have trouble communicating with his team?
items.speak: Does your boss have trouble communicating with his team?
items.secondary: ¿Tu jefe tiene problemas para comunicarse con su equipo?

audio_blocks.content_after:
**Notes:**

- Always **have trouble + gerund**, never the infinitive: *I have trouble **understanding** you*, not ~~to understand~~.
- **Much** doesn't sit comfortably in the affirmative — *a lot of* is the safer default across countable, uncountable, affirmative, negative and interrogative: ~~Yes, I had much trouble~~ → *Yes, I had **a lot of** trouble.* *Much* still works fine in questions and negatives: *Did you have **much** trouble...? I didn't have **much** trouble...*
- Don't contract **have** when it's the main verb meaning *tener* (possession): *I **have** a stapler*, not ~~I've a stapler~~. Only contract *have* when it's the auxiliary of the present perfect: *I've been to Rome.*

title: English with Kyle
topic: Mixed Translations · Talk Into/Out Of & Make Out vs. Catch · To Be Worth · Mastering the Interrogative

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| ¿A quién estás esperando? | Who are you waiting for? |
| Estábamos esperándolos hasta las tres. | We were waiting for them until three o'clock. |
| Nos quedamos levantados hasta las tantas. | We stayed up late. / We stayed up into the wee hours. |
| Nos quedamos por ahí hasta las tantas. | We stayed out late. |
| ¿Cómo puedo transmitirles la importancia de esto? | How can I convey to them how important this is? / How can I get the importance of this across to them? |
| Ella me habló hasta convencerme. | She talked me into it. |

**Key notes:**

- **Preposition stranding:** *who are you waiting **for**?* — never *for who are you waiting?* nor *who are you waiting?* on its own. The preposition goes at the end.
- **Word order with pronouns:** *we were waiting **for them***, not *we were waiting them for* — same pattern as *I did **it for you***, not *I did for you it*.
- **the wee hours** (*wee* = small, from Scottish English) = *la madrugada*, the very early hours of the morning (1, 2, 3 a.m.).
- **to stay up** (*mantenerte despierto*) vs. **to stay out** (*quedarte fuera de casa*) — two different phrasal verbs built on *stay*, both used for *nos quedamos... hasta las tantas* depending on whether you stayed home or went out.
- **to convey** = *transmitir* (information/ideas) — reserve **to transmit** for signals/broadcasts (*a radio transmitter, to transmit a frequency*), not for conveying importance or ideas.

sections.title: 2. Phrasal Verbs: Talk Into/Out Of & Make Out vs. Catch
sections.content:
**to talk someone into something** = to convince someone *to* do something (*convencer a alguien de hacer algo*):

- She talked me into it. I didn't want to do it, but she talked me into it.
- I talked her into it.
- We talked them into it. They weren't going to buy the new computer, but we talked them into it.
- I wasn't going to stay so late, but they talked me into it.

**to talk someone out of something** = to convince someone *not* to do something:

- He was going to quit the company until we talked him out of it. We convinced him not to do it.

---

**make out** vs. **catch** — both mean *to manage to perceive/understand something with difficulty*, but they split by sense:

| Verb | Sense | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **make out** | visual — reading/seeing something | I can see the words, but I can't make it out. |
| **catch** | audio — understanding speech | I can't catch what they're saying. |

Don't mix them up: you *catch* what someone says, but you *make out* what's written or barely visible.

sections.title: 3. To Be Worth
sections.content:
**Structure:** *to be worth* must be followed by a **noun**, a **pronoun**, or a **gerund** (verb+ing) — never by *to + infinitive*.

- ❌ ~~Is it worth to invest in jewels?~~ ✅ **Is it worth investing in jewels?**
- ❌ ~~I don't think Polish is worth to learn.~~ ✅ **I don't think Polish is worth learning.**
- Don't forget the verb **to be**: *A Tesla **is** worth more than a Renault* (not *a Tesla worth more...*).

**Basic uses:**

- *It's worth it. / It isn't worth it.* — I don't think taking a Polish course is worth it.
- *It's worth more / it's worth less* (comparisons of value): My phone is worth more than my pen. Knowing English is worth more than knowing Icelandic.
- *It's worth the price/effort*, *it's worth doing/knowing/having*: A good flashlight is worth having. A university degree is worth having.

**Avoid repeating the object:** once the noun is the subject, don't repeat it as a pronoun after the preposition.

- ❌ ~~Parking spaces aren't worth investing in them.~~ ✅ **Parking spaces aren't worth investing in.**
- This also works as a question: *Are parking spaces worth investing in?*

**Vocabulary — the trades** (*los oficios*): electrician, plumber, construction worker. Kyle's example: learning a trade is worth it because these jobs will never be replaced by AI — you finish a relatively short course, start working (and earning) young, and can eventually hire people and run your own business, instead of spending years at university before earning money.

**Examples from the chat:**

- I think investment in gold is worth it because its value never drops.
- It's worth living day by day because you don't know what might happen tomorrow.
- Being able to express myself in Polish would have been useful, given that I had gone to Krakow to work on projects, but the English I knew was worth it, as it saved me time.
- The barbecue I bought last year is really worth it on weekends for any kind of cookout.

title: English with Kyle
topic: Reading: No Friday Night Plans? (CNN) · Finish/Start/Stop + -ing · Hype vs. Hyper & Wary vs. Weary

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| ¿Cómo te pasó eso? | How did that happen to you? |
| Me lío con ese tiempo verbal. | I get mixed up with that verb tense. |
| Acabo de terminar de escribir más de 4,000 frases. | I've just finished writing more than 4,000 sentences. |
| ¿Qué quieres decir? | What do you mean? |
| Si yo supiera su nombre, le llamaría. | If I knew his name, I'd call him. |
| El ganar no es lo más importante. | Winning isn't the most important thing. |
| Frótalo con algodón. | Rub it with cotton. |
| Deberías habérmelo dicho. | You should have told me. |

**Key notes:**

- **to get mixed up with** (*confundirse con*) — for a specific pair of things/people you can also say **to get them mixed up**: there were two twin brothers, and sometimes I got them mixed up.
- **I've just finished writing...** — present perfect with *just*; **finish** is always followed by **-ing**, never *to + infinitive* (see Section 3).
- **If I knew his name, I'd call him.** — second conditional (*si* + past simple, *would* + infinitive), Kyle's favorite conditional.
- **Winning isn't the most important thing.** — *el ganar* behaves as a noun in Spanish, so English uses the **gerund noun** (the *-ing* form acting as a noun), not the infinitive *to win*.
- **Affirmative → Negative → Interrogative drill:** take one sentence through all three forms — *You should have told me.* → *You shouldn't have told me.* → *Should you have told me?* — a good way to build agility with a structure.

sections.title: 2. Reading: No Friday Night Plans? — Vocabulary
sections.content:
Kyle read and discussed a CNN article about the rise of in-person "social reading" events — people gathering in groups to read quietly together instead of alone at home, on the subway, or on a sun lounger. Below is the vocabulary and phrasing covered along the way.

| Word / Phrase | Spanish | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| a pastime | un pasatiempo | a hobby or activity done for enjoyment |
| best enjoyed (alone) | mejor disfrutado (a solas) | a participle structure describing how something is typically experienced |
| hipster-filled (neighborhood) | barrio lleno de hipsters | a compound adjective — two words joined by a hyphen to form one adjective |
| attendees | asistentes | the people who attend an event |
| had brought / they'd brought | habían traído | past perfect — an action completed before another past action |
| curated (playlist) | cuidadosamente elaborado | carefully chosen and put together |
| to hold / to be held | celebrar, tener lugar | the event is held at a nightclub = the event takes place at a nightclub |
| a confluence of trends | una confluencia de tendencias | several trends coming together at the same time |
| a getaway | una escapada | a short trip away from daily life |
| a retreat | un retiro | a short escape to disconnect — personal or corporate, not a big trip |
| (from) cover to cover | de portada a portada | reading a whole book from start to finish |
| a (pub) crawl | una ronda de bares | visiting several bars in one night on a schedule — "the crawl" is also a swimming stroke |
| to bemoan (something) | quejarse de, lamentar | to complain about or express sadness about something, close to "to moan" |
| a slew (of) | un montón, un mogollón de | a large quantity of something |
| to plummet | caer en picado | to fall sharply |
| a backdrop | un telón de fondo | the context or situation behind something |
| sold out | agotado | no tickets or spots left |
| a surge | un subidón, una subida | a sudden increase |
| to lug (something) around | acarrear, cargar con algo pesado | to carry something heavy — the root of the word "luggage" |
| performative | de cara a la galería | done for show, to signal something to others, rather than out of genuine interest |
| a self-fulfilling cycle | un ciclo que se retroalimenta | a cycle that reinforces itself and causes its own continuation |

sections.title: 3. Finish, Start & Stop + -ing/to
sections.content:
**finish** takes **-ing** only — never *to + infinitive*:

- I've just finished writing more than 4,000 sentences. ✅
- ❌ I have already finished to write 4,000 sentences.

**start** takes either **-ing** or **to + infinitive** — both are correct:

- Start walking. / Start to walk. — no difference in meaning.

**stop** changes meaning depending on the form:

| Form | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **stop** + **-ing** | to cease doing something | I stopped driving. / I stopped walking. |
| **stop** + **to** + infinitive | to pause *in order to* do something else | I stopped to take a break. / I stopped to have lunch. |

**Tone note:** *I've just finished* (*acabo de*) signals something very recently completed, while *I've already finished* (*ya he terminado*) carries a slightly different tone — more like relief or emphasis that it's done.

sections.title: 4. Hype vs. Hyper & Wary vs. Weary
sections.content:
Two easily-confused word pairs from the discussion:

**hype (noun/verb) vs. hyper- (prefix)**

- **hype** (noun) = *mucha promoción, mucho bombo* — exaggerated excitement or promotion around something, often with little real substance: it's all hype, there's a lot of hype around AI.
- **to hype (something) up** (verb) = *promocionar, fomentar interés* — to promote or generate interest in something: you can hype up The English Collective with your friends.
- **hyper-** (prefix) = *muy, súper* — intensifies an adjective: hyper-aware = muy consciente.

**wary vs. weary**

| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **wary (of)** | cauteloso, receloso — you don't fully trust something | I'm wary of people who call to sell me something over the phone. |
| **weary (of)** | cansado, harto — tired of something | People are growing weary of doom scrolling and dating apps. |

They sound similar but aren't the same: *wary* = cautious/distrustful, *weary* = tired/fed up.

title: English with Kyle
topic: Verb Vocabulary / The Future Perfect Tense

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Acabamos de recibir la noticia. | We've just received the news. |
| Yo acababa de comer cuando él llegó. | I had just eaten when he arrived. |
| ¿Has rellenado el impreso? | Have you filled out the form? |
| ¿De qué impreso estás hablando? | What form are you talking about? |
| Quiero que solicites un trabajo. | I want you to apply for a job. |
| ¿Qué quieres que diga? | What do you want me to say? |
| ¿Dónde quieres que lo pongamos? | Where do you want us to put it? |
| Él quiere que yo lo busque. | He wants me to look for it. |

**Key notes:**

- **acabar de hacer algo** (*to have just done something*) → present perfect with *just* when the reference point is now (*we've just received...*), but **past perfect** when the reference point is itself in the past: *yo acababa de comer cuando él llegó* → *I had just eaten when he arrived*.
- **the news** is always singular and uncountable, always with an S: *the news*, never *the new*. To quantify it: *a piece of news* / *some news*.
- **to fill in** (rellenar cada casilla/espacio — one field at a time) vs. **to fill out** (rellenar el formulario entero — complete the whole form): *In order to fill it out, we had to fill in a lot of details.*
- Ending a question with a preposition is completely normal in English: *What form are you talking about?* — not a mistake, despite what some old-school rules claim.
- **I want you to...** — never *I want that you...*: see Section 2 for the full structure.

sections.title: 2. I Want You To... — The Accusative Structure
sections.content:
**Common mistake:** ❌ ~~I want that you...~~ — Spanish *quiero que* does **not** translate word-for-word into English.

**Structure:** subject + verb (want/need) + object (person) + **to** + infinitive — sometimes called the **accusative structure**.

- I want you to apply for a job. (*Quiero que solicites un trabajo*)
- The government wants me to pay taxes.
- I want you to speak in English.
- My students want me to offer more classes.
- They want us to help them.
- I want you to listen to me. (*Quiero que me escuches*)
- What do you want me to say? (*¿Qué quieres que diga?*)
- When do you want it to be here? (*¿Cuándo quieres que esté aquí?*)
- How many do you want me to bring? (*¿Cuántos quieres que traiga?*) — remember **bring here, take there**
- Where do you want us to put it? (*¿Dónde quieres que lo pongamos?*)
- He wants me to look for it. (*Él quiere que yo lo busque*)

Pattern to internalize: **subject → object → infinitive.** There's a dedicated grammar resource on this structure in the Resource Center for extra practice.

sections.title: 3. Verb Vocabulary — Picture Descriptions
sections.content:
Seven pictures, seven verbs — a recurring warm-up exercise Kyle returns to periodically to build up verb vocabulary.

| # | What's happening | Key vocabulary |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | A barista is pouring cream into a coffee | **to pour** (echar un líquido) |
| 2 | A man is pushing/sliding a couch across the floor, not lifting it | **to push**, **to slide**, **to move** (furniture) |
| 3 | A woman is looking at the scenery through binoculars | **to look through** binoculars |
| 4 | A man is sprinkling seasoning onto meat | **to season**, **to sprinkle**, **a dash (of)**, **a pinch (of)** |
| 5 | A woman is struggling to control her umbrella on a windy day | **to struggle with** |
| 6 | A man is daydreaming instead of studying | **to daydream** |
| 7 | A man is varnishing/painting/resurfacing a chair | **to varnish**, **to paint**, **to resurface** |

**Extra vocabulary notes:**

- **to watch** (something with motion, e.g. a whale, a movie) vs. **to look at** (something still) vs. **to look through** (binoculars, a telescope).
- **a dash (of)** → un poquito — works with both liquids (*a dash of red wine*) and solids (*a dash of salt*); **a pinch (of)** → una pizca, only for solids.
- **to enhance** → mejorar: *I added a dash of hot sauce to enhance the flavor.*
- **to hover** (over something with the mouse/cursor) → pasar por encima — e.g. hovering over a chat message reveals an edit option.
- **dream of** vs. **dream about**: very close in meaning, but *dream of* leans toward a wish/aspiration (*he's dreaming of winning the lottery*), while *dream about* leans toward something more concrete you spend time thinking about (*I dreamt about being with my family*).

sections.title: 4. The Future Perfect Tense
sections.content:
**Structure:** *will have* + past participle (or *will have been* + -ing for the continuous form) — describes something that will be completed, or will have been going on, by a specific point in the future.

**Building the timeline** (Kyle's example):

- 10 minutes ago: *I had been here for 30 minutes.* (past perfect)
- Now: *I have been here for 40 minutes.* (present perfect)
- 20 minutes from now: *I will have been here for 60 minutes.* (future perfect continuous)

**More examples:**

- By the end of the year, Pedro Sánchez will have been president for nine years.
- By this time next year, he will have been president for nine years.
- In two years' time, he will have been the prime minister for three years.
- By the end of the year, my sister will have finished her degree.
- In 20 years' time, I will have finished paying off my mortgage. / I will have paid off my mortgage.
- In six months' time, I'll have been working on this project for a year.
- I will have been married for 25 years in five years' time.

**Time expressions with the Saxon genitive:** *in two years' time*, *in five years' time*, *in six months' time* — the apostrophe-S goes on the time period.

**Past vs. future — watch the tense of the trigger clause:**

| Trigger clause | Main clause tense | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *By the time he **got** there...* (past) | past perfect | *...she had been waiting for two hours.* |
| *By the time he **gets** there...* (future) | future perfect | *...she will have been waiting for two hours.* |

**Vocabulary:** **to pay off** (a debt) → liquidar la deuda, to finish making payments on something.

title: English with Kyle
topic: Giving a Talk (Imperatives) · Reflexive Pronouns · Should / Shouldn't · Had Better · Mastering the Interrogative

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
*Theme: tips for giving a talk or a speech.* All of these are **negative/positive imperatives** — infinitive without *to*, and no subject.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| No abandones. | Don't give up. |
| No des tu brazo a torcer. | Don't give in. / Don't back down. |
| Asegúrate de que la gente te oiga. | Make sure (that) the people hear you. |
| No te pongas nervioso. | Don't get nervous. |
| No pierdas la calma. | Don't lose your cool. |
| Trata de causar una buena impresión. | Try to make a good impression. |
| No dejes que te pongan nervioso. | Don't let them make you nervous. |
| Empieza el discurso con una anécdota. | Start the speech with an anecdote. / Start the speech with a story. |
| Si no se ríen, no te preocupes por ello. | If they don't laugh, don't worry about it. |
| Asegúrate de que tienes su atención. | Make sure (that) you have their attention. |

**Key notes:**

- **give up** (*abandonar, rendirse*) vs. **give in** / **back down** (*dar tu brazo a torcer, ceder*) — similar but different phrasal verbs. (*"I won't back down"* — Tom Petty.)
- **make sure (that)...** — *that* is optional.
- **the people** vs. **people:** *make sure **the** people hear you* — here we mean a specific audience (the people at your talk), so use the article. With people in general, no article.
- **nervous** — pronounce the final **s** clearly: /ˈnɜːr-vəs/, not *nervou-sh*. Think of Elvis: *Was Elvis nervous?*
- **to lose your cool** = *perder la calma*. **To stay cool** = *mantener la calma*. (*Cool* can also mean *fresquito* — *cool at night* — or *guay*.)
- **to make an impression** (not *cause an impression*): *make a good / bad impression*.
- **a talk** = *una charla*; **a speech** = *un discurso*. A brief talk is a **short talk** — not a *small talk*: **small talk** is inconsequential chat to avoid an awkward silence (*"Qué calor hoy, ¿no?"* with your neighbour in the lift).
- **a story** (consonant sound → *a*) but **an anecdote** (vowel sound → *an*).
- **su atención** is ambiguous in Spanish — in English choose: *his / her / their attention*.

sections.title: 2. Reflexive Pronouns (Describing Pictures)
sections.content:
Describing pictures with **reflexive pronouns** (*myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves*) and the **reciprocal pronoun** *each other*.

| # | Picture | Sentence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | A man in front of a mirror | He's looking at **himself** in the mirror. He's talking to **himself**. |
| 2 | A woman at a mirror | She's looking at **herself** in the mirror, and she's putting on her earrings. |
| 3 | Two people chatting | They're talking to **each other**. |
| 4 | A woman stretching | She's stretching. *(not ~~she's stretching herself~~)* |
| 5 | A man at a mirror, just out of the shower | He's looking at **himself** in the mirror. He's fixing / drying **his** hair. |
| 6 | Two hikers on a mountain | They're talking to **each other**. They're standing on a mountain, going hiking. |
| 7 | A hiker bending down | He's tying **his** shoelaces. *(not ~~he's tying himself~~)* |

**Key notes:**

- **Reflexive** (*-self / -selves*): the subject does the action to itself — *he's looking at himself*.
- **Reciprocal** (*each other*): two or more people do the action to one another — *they're talking to each other* (*se hablan el uno al otro*). *Themselves* would mean each one is talking to himself/herself.
- Many actions that are reflexive in Spanish (*estirarse, atarse los cordones, secarse el pelo*) are **not** reflexive in English: *she's stretching, he's tying his shoes, he's drying his hair*. English uses the **possessive** (*his hair, her earrings*) instead.
- Don't mix genders: *he's tying **his** shoes* (not *his shoes herself*).
- *putting on* **her** earrings — *put on* = *ponerse* (clothes, jewellery).

For more practice, see the **Reflexive Pronouns** lesson (with audio translation challenge) under *Grammar Lessons* in the Resource Center.

sections.title: 3. Should / Shouldn't — Giving Advice
sections.content:
**should / shouldn't + infinitive (without *to*)** = giving advice (*deberías / no deberías*).

| # | Picture | Advice |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | A boy crossing the street looking at his phone | He **should** look both ways before crossing the street. He **shouldn't** cross when the light is red. He **shouldn't** cross the road while looking at his mobile phone. He **should** look at the traffic light before crossing. |
| 2 | A girl driving far from the steering wheel | She **should** fasten her seatbelt. / She **should** wear a seatbelt while driving. She **shouldn't** drive so far from the wheel — she **should** sit closer to the steering wheel. |
| 3 | Two climbers on a mountain | The guy in red **should** slow down. He **shouldn't** go so fast. His friend **should** tell him to slow down. They **should** hire a guide to help them climb the mountain. |
| 4 | A girl eating junk food at her computer | She **shouldn't** eat so much junk food. She **should** keep a healthy diet. |
| 5 | A boy playing video games and eating pizza late at night | He **shouldn't** stay up so late. He **shouldn't** be playing video games for such a long time. He **shouldn't** eat junk food late at night. |
| 6 | A girl on the beach | She **should** apply plenty of sunscreen. |
| 7 | A sick boy | He **should** take care of himself. He **should** get some rest. |

**Key notes:**

- **to fasten a seatbelt** = *abrochar el cinturón* (not *tie* — *tie* = *atar*).
- **the traffic light** / **the crosswalk** — not ~~semaphore~~ (Spanglish for *semáforo*).
- **sunscreen** or **sun cream** = *crema solar* — *cream* ends in **m**.
- **hire a guide to climb** — after *to*, use the infinitive: *to help them climb the mountain*.
- **under the weather** = feeling a bit ill.

sections.title: 4. Had Better
sections.content:
**had better ('d better) + infinitive (without *to*)** = a **stronger** suggestion than *should*, often with a warning (*más vale que...*).

- ❌ ~~He had better to look both ways.~~ ✅ **He had better look both ways.** — the most common mistake is adding *to*.
- Negative: **had better not** + infinitive — *He'd better not cross without looking.*
- Very often followed by a **potential consequence** with ***because otherwise...*** (*porque si no...*).
- In fast speech *had* almost disappears: *He**'d** better... / He better...*

**Examples (same pictures as the "should" exercise):**

1. He'd better look both ways before crossing the street. He'd better not look at his mobile phone while crossing the street. He'd better be careful.
2. She'd better wear her seatbelt, because otherwise she could get hurt in an accident. She'd better sit closer to the steering wheel, because otherwise she'll have a reduced reaction time.
3. They'd better not go too fast. They'd better not get lost on the mountain.
4. She'd better not eat so much junk food, because otherwise she could have high cholesterol. She'd better change her diet, because otherwise she'll weigh 100 kilos in 10 years.
5. He'd better go to bed. He'd better not stay up all night playing video games, because otherwise he could have health problems.
6. She'd better wear sunscreen, because otherwise she could get a sunburn. She'd better not stay out in the sun too long.
7. You'd better go to bed and stay warm under the blankets.

sections.title: 5. Mastering the Interrogative
sections.content:
| Statement | Question |
|---|---|
| The monastery was built in the 12th century. | When was the monastery built? |
| It was Steven's fault. | Whose fault was it? |
| Peter knows the combination to the lock. | Who knows the combination to the lock? |
| He did it last week. | When did he do it? |
| The report is 36 pages long. | How long is the report? |
| You can learn the process by observation. | How can I learn the process? |
| We have 100 envelopes left. | How many envelopes do we have left? |
| That type of meeting usually lasts one hour. | How long does that type of meeting usually last? |
| I expect him back here in a few minutes. | When do you expect him back here? |

**Key notes:**

- **Whose + noun:** the noun goes directly after *whose* — ***Whose fault** was it?* (*¿De quién fue la culpa?*), not ~~Whose was the fault?~~ Same with *Whose book is this? Whose pen is that?*
- **Who** as the subject → no auxiliary: *Who **knows** the combination?* (not *Who does know...*).
- **Passive questions:** *When **was** the monastery **built**?*

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
*Theme: the many uses of **get**.*

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Me estoy acostumbrando a ello. | I'm getting used to it. |
| Bájate del coche. | Get out of the car. |
| Bájate del autobús. | Get off the bus. |
| Súbete al autobús. | Get on the bus. |
| Súbete al coche. | Get into the car. |
| Enfermé durante el viaje. | I got sick / I got ill during the trip. |
| Estuve enfermo durante tres días. | I was sick for three days. |
| Llegué de vuelta anoche. | I got back last night. |
| Me levanté temprano. | I got up early. |
| Oscurece pronto en invierno. | It gets dark early in winter. |
| El agua se pone caliente si la hierves. | Water gets hot if you boil it. |
| Si sales ahora, te mojarás. | If you go out now, you'll get wet. |
| Tu salud está empeorando. | Your health is getting worse. |

**Key notes:**

- **Three kinds of *used to*:** *used to* + infinitive (past habit — *I used to live in Canada*), **be used to** (*estar acostumbrado* — *I'm used to this chair*), **get used to** (*acostumbrarse*, the process — *I'm getting used to this computer*).
- **get into / get out of** → enclosed, smaller spaces: a car, a taxi, a lift. **get on / get off** → public / mass transport: a bus, a train, a boat, a plane. Learn the opposites together: anything you *get into*, you later *get out of*; anything you *get on*, you later *get off*.
  - Rule of thumb from the chat: if you can stand up inside, it's *on*; if not, it's *in*. (A lift can take either.)
  - **hop on, hop off** — sightseeing buses you can jump on and off all day.
  - Figurative: *to get into trouble*, *to get out of jail*.
- **durante** → **during** + an event (*during the trip*) but **for** + a period of time (*for three days*).
- **early vs. soon:** **early** compares with the *usual/scheduled* time (*the class started early — at 8:15 instead of 8:30*; *it gets dark early in winter*). **soon** = only a short time from *now* (*it'll be Wednesday soon*). ❌ ~~It gets dark soon in winter.~~
- ❌ ~~In winter it used to get dark early~~ — that means *antes oscurecía*. For a general truth use the **present simple**: *It gets dark early in winter.* The **present continuous** is for what's happening now: *Look, it's getting dark.* / *It's getting darker.*
- **if I'm not mistaken** = *si no me equivoco*.

sections.title: 2. Describing a Picture: A Riverside Café
sections.content:
Describing an AI-generated picture: a **riverside café in a European city** on an autumn afternoon.

**On the table (left):**

- There's a **croissant** on a **plate**, a **notebook** with a **pen on top of it**, and a **cup of coffee**.
- **a cup of coffee** (the drink you order) ≠ **a coffee cup** (the empty container). The one next to the backpack is a **travel mug**.
- There are some **blankets on the back of the chair**. There's a **backpack** and a **city map**.

**Along the river:**

- There's a man with a hat **playing the guitar** — a street performer is a **busker**, and playing music on the street for money is **busking** (Halifax used to hold a *Busker Festival*).
- A woman is **sitting on a bench**. The bench is **facing the river** (facing out, not in). She's looking at the beautiful autumn view.
- A **riverboat** is **sailing / cruising down the river**; it's going to go **under the bridge**.
- People are **walking away from us** on the **cobblestone** street. The street is **lined with trees** — there are trees **along the canal**.
- There's a **bicycle leaning against a post**, and some **flowers**.
- A few **pigeons** are **pecking at the crumbs** on the ground.
- It's a lovely autumn afternoon **by the riverbank**, along the **promenade**.

**In the distance:**

- There's a **castle on the hill across the river**, a **cathedral**, and a **tower** (a bit like Seville's Torre del Oro).

sections.title: 3. Phrasal Verbs with 'In'
sections.content:
**The trick:** learn phrasal verbs by **particle + concept**, not one by one — one concept unlocks many verbs. And learn the **opposites** together: *up/down, in/out, on/off*.

**in vs. into:** *into* always has **motion** (*the pen is going **into** the glass*); *in* is the position once it's there (*the water is **in** the glass*). The opposite of *into* is **out of** (never ~~out to~~).

### 1. In = Entering (*entrar*)

| Phrasal verb | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **come in / go in** | enter (from outside) | *He came in without knocking.* · *If I were you, I wouldn't go in there.* |
| **get in** | manage to enter; get into a vehicle; arrive | *She got into the taxi and gave the driver her address.* · *What time did you get in?* |
| **run in** | enter running | *He ran into the shop.* · *They run into the bullring* (Pamplona). |
| **walk in** | enter walking | *I walked into the supermarket this morning at about 10:00.* |
| **break in** | enter by force / to steal | *Has your house ever been broken into?* |
| **phase in** | introduce in stages | *The project will be phased in so that everyone can get used to it.* |

### 2. In = Assimilating (*asimilar*)

| Phrasal verb | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **take in** (separable) | absorb / understand information | *That's a lot of information to take in.* · *Did he take in everything you said?* · *It was difficult for him to take everything in.* |
| **sink in** (intransitive — the information is the subject) | be fully understood | *Let that sink in.* · *I don't think what I said sank in.* · *It took a split second for that to sink in.* |

- ❌ ~~I've taken in dancing~~ → ✅ **I've taken up dancing** — *take up* = start a hobby. *Take in* is for information and concepts.
- **a split second** = *un santiamén, un pispás* — also **in the blink of an eye**.

### 3. In = Substituting (*sustituir*)

| Phrasal verb | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **fill in for** someone | substitute temporarily | *If I can't do my class on Thursday, I might ask Julia to fill in for me.* · *Can you fill in for me while I'm away?* · *The vice president filled in for the president.* |
| **stand in for** someone | substitute temporarily | *I had to stand in for him when he didn't show up.* · *The cameraman had to stand in for the news anchor.* |

- A **stand-in** (noun) = someone who substitutes temporarily, e.g. for an actor at rehearsals.
- Different meaning: **fill in** a gap / a hole / a form = *rellenar*.

### 4. In = Delivering (*entregar*) — towards a central point

| Phrasal verb | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **hand in** | deliver by hand, yourself | *When do we have to hand in the final project?* · *You were supposed to hand it in last week.* |
| **send in** | deliver by post/email — out of your hands for a while | *Send in your application.* · *We sent out 20 invitations, but they only sent in 10 responses.* |
| **turn in** | hand over (often something illegal, to the authorities) | *If you turn in your guns at the police station today, you won't get a fine.* |

- Opposite: **send out** — *We sent out 1,000 emails, and they sent in their responses.*
- **turn over** ≠ *turn in*: *turn over* = *dar la vuelta*.

title: English with Kyle
topic: Reported Speech · Phrasal Verbs with Into · Slip vs. Slide · Movies vs. Films

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| No discutamos hoy. | Let's not argue today. |
| Hay petróleo en la superficie. | There's oil on the surface. |
| Como sal solo con mariscos. | I eat salt only with seafood / shellfish. |
| Puedes resbalar y hacerte daño. | You can slip and hurt yourself. |
| Es más fácil correr cuesta abajo que cuesta arriba. | It's easier to run downhill than uphill. |
| Mi hermana quiere hablar contigo. | My sister wants to talk to you. |

**Key notes:**

- **discutir ≠ discuss.** *Discutir* (with anger) = **to argue**: *Let's not argue today · We were arguing about football.* **To discuss** = simply talk about a topic, calmly.
- **on the surface** — not ~~in~~ the surface. **oil** (more American) / **petrol** (more British).
- **only — word order matters.** Put *only* right before the part it limits:
  - ✅ *I eat salt **only with seafood*** (the only time I use salt is with seafood).
  - ⚠ *I **only eat** salt with seafood* sounds like *lo único que como es sal con marisco*.
  - *just* also works here, meaning *nada más que*: *I eat salt just with seafood.* (But *I just ate* = *acabo de comer*.)
  - *Solo como marisco los domingos* → *I only eat seafood on Sundays.*
- **seafood** = *pescado y marisco* in general · **shellfish** = *marisco* (shells).
- **slip vs. slide:** **slip** = *resbalar*, usually **by accident**; **slide** = *deslizar*, usually **on purpose** (e.g. skating on ice). A *Slip 'N Slide* was a wet plastic sheet kids ran and slid on.
- **downhill** = *cuesta abajo* · **uphill** = *cuesta arriba*. Use **to + infinitive** after *it's easier*: *It's easier **to run** downhill than uphill* (or *Running downhill is easier than running uphill*). *Running uphill is **harder*** — not ~~more hard~~.
  - **downhill skiing** vs. **cross-country skiing** (*esquí de fondo*).
- **talk to** someone: *My sister wants to talk to you.*

sections.title: 2. Reported Speech
sections.content:
**Reported speech** = reporting what someone said, like in a newspaper. It has to be able to *live in the past and always be true* — whether you say it tomorrow or 100 years from now. So we **freeze it in time**: move the verb **one step back** and remove references to *now*.

*"I like ice cream."* → *Kyle said that he **liked** ice cream.*
*"I ate a hamburger yesterday."* → *Kyle said that he **had eaten** a hamburger **the day before**.*
*"I'm going to the beach tomorrow."* → *Kyle said he **was going** to the beach **the following day**.*

### Tense Backshift

| Direct speech | Reported speech |
|---|---|
| present simple (*I like*) | past simple (*he liked*) |
| present continuous (*I'm planning*) | past continuous (*he was planning*) |
| present perfect (*I've been*) | past perfect (*he had been*) |
| past simple (*I ate*) | past perfect (*he had eaten*) |
| will (*I'll be*) | would (*he would be*) |
| am going to (*I'm going to make*) | was going to (*he was going to make*) |
| imperative (*Don't worry*) | told + object + (not) to (*he told her **not to worry***) |

### Time & Place Words

| Direct speech | Reported speech |
|---|---|
| tomorrow | the next day / the following day |
| yesterday | the day before |
| this summer / this year | that summer / that year |
| next year / next week | the following year / the following week |
| here | there |
| come | go |

### Reporting Questions

- Yes/no questions → **asked (someone) if** + statement word order: *"Do you enjoy visiting national parks?"* → *He asked him **if he enjoyed** visiting national parks.*
- Wh- questions → **asked (someone) + wh-word** + statement word order: *"How long will you be here?"* → *She asked him **how long he would be** there.*
- ❌ ~~She asked to him~~ → ✅ *She asked him* (no *to* after *ask*).

### Conversation 1 — Philip & Nigel

| Direct speech | Reported speech |
|---|---|
| **Philip:** "Have you ever been to Yellowstone Park?" | Philip asked Nigel if he had ever been to Yellowstone Park. |
| **Nigel:** "No, I've never been there." | Nigel said that he had never been there. |
| **Philip:** "Do you enjoy visiting national parks?" | Philip asked him if he enjoyed visiting national parks. |
| **Nigel:** "I don't know. I haven't been to one in 20 years." | Nigel said that he didn't know and that he hadn't been to one in 20 years. |
| **Philip:** "Tomorrow I'm going to make reservations for you and your wife." | Philip said that the following day he was going to make reservations for him and his wife. |
| **Nigel:** "Are you sure my wife will like visiting a park?" | Nigel asked Philip if he was sure that his wife would like visiting a park. |
| **Philip:** "Everyone enjoys Yellowstone Park." | Philip said that everyone enjoyed Yellowstone Park. |

### Conversation 2 — Inês & François

| Direct speech | Reported speech |
|---|---|
| **Inês:** "Are you planning to come to Seville this summer?" | Inês asked François if he was planning to go to Seville that summer. |
| **François:** "I've already booked a ticket for late June." | François said that he had already booked a ticket for late June. |
| **Inês:** "How long will you be here?" | She asked him how long he would be there. |
| **François:** "I want to learn Spanish, so I'll be there for two months." | He said that he wanted to learn Spanish, so he would be there for two months. |
| **Inês:** "Do you want me to look for an apartment for you?" | She asked him if he wanted her to look for an apartment for him. |
| **François:** "Don't worry, I have a friend in Seville who has an extra bedroom." | He told her not to worry because he had a friend in Seville who had an extra bedroom. |
| **Inês:** "You're going to like living here." | She said that he was going to like living there. |

- **here → there / come → go:** Inês is in Seville, so she says *here* and *come*; François isn't, so he says *there*. In the report, we're not in Seville, so it's always **there** and **go**.
- Watch the pronouns: *She asked **him** if **he** wanted **her** to look for an apartment for **him**.*

sections.title: 3. Phrasal Verbs with 'Into'
sections.content:
### More with 'In' (review)

| Phrasal verb | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **stuff in** | *meter con fuerza* — force something in | *The robber stuffed the stolen money in his sock.* · *Stuff some more stuffing in that turkey.* · *How are we going to stuff all that food in the fridge?* |
| **plug in** | *enchufar* | *Plug it in over there.* · *There's already something plugged in over there.* · *Plug in the power bar first.* |

- **stuffing** = *el relleno* (e.g. of a Thanksgiving turkey).
- **a power bar** (Canadian) / **a multi-socket plug** = *un ladrón*.

### In vs. Into

**into** always involves **motion**; **in** is the position once you're there.

- *The spoon is going **into** the cup.* → *The spoon is **in** the cup.* (never ~~it is into~~)
- *I came **into** the room before class.* → *I'm **in** the room.* · *She went **into** the bedroom.*

But some phrasal verbs use *into* with a special meaning:

### Bump Into / Run Into

**bump into / run into** = *toparse con, encontrarse con* (a person, by chance) — or *chocar contra* (physical contact).

- *I was in Marbella, and I ran into David on the beach.*
- *Guess who I bumped into the other day?*
- *She bumped into a colleague on the weekend.*
- *He was surprised to bump into his old boss.*
- Physical: *He bumped into the glass door.* · *I ran into a post with my car.*

### Turn Into

**turn into** = *convertirse en* · **be turned into** = *ser convertido / adaptado a*.

- *Clark Kent can turn into Superman.* · *Bruce Wayne can turn into Batman.*
- *After his accident, he turned into a very angry person.*
- *He was new in the office, but within a year, he turned into an expert in the industry.*
- *The book was turned into a movie.* (*se adaptó al cine*)
- *Elvis's house, Graceland, was turned into a museum.*
- *He turned the car into a convertible in 20 seconds.*

**turn out (to be)** ≠ *turn into* — **turn out** = *resultar (ser)*, end with a particular result:

- *Everyone thought it was going to rain, but it turned out to be a beautiful day.*
- *We thought the project was going to fail, but it turned out to be the most profitable project we had done in years.*
- *In the end, the police officer turned out to be the one who stole the money.*

### Look Into

**look into** = *investigar, examinar* — usually a **light** investigation (for something serious like a murder, say **investigate**).

- *Someone stole the money. We're looking into it.*
- *I'll ask my friend to look into it for you.*
- *He's looking into his family's history.*
- *Have we looked into all the possibilities?*
- *We're looking into who put more salt in the stew.*

sections.title: 4. Movies vs. Films & Blockbusters
sections.content:
- **movies** → Hollywood, big stars (Arnold Schwarzenegger, Tom Cruise, Sylvester Stallone), big budgets.
- **films** → more artistic, story-driven, often smaller budgets — what you see at the **Cannes Film Festival**. **a short film** = *un corto*.
- **a blockbuster** = *un taquillazo, un gran éxito* (like the old video rental store *Blockbuster Video*, before streaming on demand).
  - Also as an adjective: *a blockbuster deal* — *When Cristiano Ronaldo was sold to another team, it was a blockbuster deal.*

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations
sections.content:
| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| No hay por qué preocuparse. | There's no need to worry. |
| Él está en camino. | He's on his way. |
| ¿Cuánto tiempo dura el curso? | How long does the course last? |
| ¿Has solicitado la beca? | Have you applied for the scholarship? |
| Somos amigos desde hace un año. | We've been friends for a year. |
| Tenemos que darle un nombre. | We have to give it a name. |
| Tendrás que invertir cierta cantidad de dinero. | You'll have to invest a certain amount of money. |
| Te daremos acciones. | We'll give you shares. |
| Echa la carta al correo. | Mail the letter. |
| Ojalá pudiera convencerle. | I wish I could convince him. |

**Key notes:**

- **There's no need to worry** is much more common than *You don't have to worry*.
- **on the way / on his way** = *de camino, en camino* (*I'm on my way*). **in the way** = *en medio* (*There's a car in the way*).
- **How long does the course last?** — a course that runs regularly. **How long will the course last?** — one specific future course.
- **ask for vs. apply for:** **ask for** = just request something (*a glass of water*). **apply for** = *solicitar* through a process, with paperwork (*a job, a scholarship*).
  - **a scholarship** = *una beca* (spelled S-C-H). A **bursary** is similar.
- **desde hace / desde → present perfect**, not present simple, because it started in the past and is still true:
  - ❌ ~~We are friends for a year~~ → ✅ **We've been friends for a year** · **We've been friends since May**.
  - *It's blue* → *It's **been** blue since I painted it.* · *Estoy aquí desde hace un año* → *I've **been** here for a year.*
  - **for** + a period (*for 24 hours*) · **since** + a point in time (*since yesterday*).
- **give it a name** — or *We have to give the dog a name*.
- **shares vs. stocks** = *acciones* — basically the same. A *share* is a portion (*a share of the pie, a share of the company*); *stocks* is the more general word.
  - Stocks = **equity** investment (you become part owner). **Bonds** = you buy the company's **debt**, and they pay you back with interest. → **debt and equity financing**.
- **I wish** + past = *ojalá*: *I wish I could convince him.*

sections.title: 3. Reported Speech: Luigi & Anna (Dictation)
sections.content:
Last week's reported speech practice, but this time **dictated** (no text in the chat): a phone-style dialogue between **Luigi** and **Anna**. Remember: go **one step back** in tense, and *tomorrow* → *the following day/morning*.

### Luigi & Anna

| Direct speech | Reported speech |
|---|---|
| **Luigi:** "Have you spoken to the man in Stuttgart?" | Luigi asked Anna if she had spoken to the man in Stuttgart. |
| **Anna:** "He's away on a business trip." | She said that he was away on a business trip. |
| **Luigi:** "When will he get back?" | He asked her when he would get back. |
| **Anna:** "His secretary told me that he will be back tomorrow morning." | Anna said that his secretary had told her that he would be back (was going to be back) the following morning. |
| **Luigi:** "Did you send him the report?" | Luigi asked if she had sent him the report. |
| **Anna:** "I sent it to him by email." | Anna said that she had sent it to him by email. |
| **Luigi:** "It's important for him to read it tomorrow." | Luigi said that it was important for him to read it the following day. |

- **is → was** (simple past, not past perfect): *He's away* → *she said he **was** away*.
- **told → had told** and **sent → had sent** (simple past → past perfect).
- **will → would**: *When will he get back?* → *when he **would** get back* (statement word order, no *will he*).
- **away on a business trip** — *on* a trip, not ~~in~~.
- ❌ ~~Luigi asked to Anna~~ → ✅ *Luigi asked Anna*.

sections.title: 4. Phrasal Verbs with 'Out'
sections.content:
Same method as *in* / *into*: learn the **concept** the particle brings, and you learn several phrasal verbs at once.

### 1. Out = Distributing (*distribuir*) — from a central point outwards

- **hand out · give out · pass out** — the opposite of **hand in / send in / pass in** (*entregar a un punto central*).
- ⚠ *pass out* also means *desmayarse* (to faint) in other contexts.

### 2. Out = Exiting (*salir, dejar un sitio*)

- **come out** (towards the speaker) · **go out** (away / at night) · **get out** (manage to leave) · **walk out · rush out · run out · drive out**.
- *Are you coming out tonight?* · *If the house is burning, you have to get out of the house.*
- *Le vi salir del baño hace cinco minutos* → **I saw him come out of the bathroom five minutes ago.** (*washroom*; Americans say *restroom*)
- *Salió de la reunión con pinta de cansado* → **He came out of the meeting looking tired.**
- *Salir del coche* → **Get out of the car.**

### 3. Out = Extinguishing (*apagar*)

| Phrasal verb | Type | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **put out** (a fire, a candle) | separable — someone does it | *The firefighters put out the fire.* |
| **blow out** (*apagar soplando*) | separable | *I blew out the candles. I blew them out on my birthday.* |
| **go out** (*apagarse* by itself) | inseparable — no object | *A fire needs oxygen, otherwise it goes out.* |

- Someone **puts it out** → it **goes out**. Oil well fires are put out with an explosion that sucks the oxygen away, so the fire goes out.
- **an oil well** = *un pozo de petróleo*.

### 4. Out = Launching (*lanzar, sacar a la venta*)

- **bring out / put out** a product (transitive) → the product **comes out** (intransitive).
- *Coca-Cola puts out new products every year.* · *They brought out a new version.*
- *After Disney bought Star Wars, they started putting out a lot more movies.* → *A lot of new movies came out.*
- **to go downhill** (figurative) = *ir a peor*: *I feel like they've gone downhill a little bit.*

### 5. Out = Withdrawing (*retirarse, echarse atrás, abandonar*)

| Phrasal verb | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **back out (of)** | *echarse atrás* of a commitment (also literally: reverse out of a parking space) | *He was engaged, and he backed out in the last week.* · *They were going to buy the company, but they backed out.* |
| **drop out (of)** | *dejar los estudios* / leave a course or program | *He dropped out of university.* · *She dropped out of the course.* |
| **pull out (of)** | withdraw | *They pulled out of the agreement.* |

- **give up** is different — for a **habit**: *I gave up smoking.* · *He gave up eating sugar.*
- **to quit cold turkey** = stop suddenly, all at once (*de golpe, del tirón*).
- **to wean yourself off** something = reduce it gradually: *I'm weaning myself off cigarettes — 20 a day, then 15, 10, 5, 1, none.*

sections.title: 1. Warm-Up Translations: Phrasal Verbs
sections.content:
Five sentences planned, ten delivered: every warm-up sentence today used a **phrasal verb**. Translate them first, then check the notes.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Pasaré por tu casa camino de la mía. | I'll pass by your house on the way to mine. |
| La buena señora falleció después de una larga enfermedad. | The good lady passed away after a long illness. |
| Me quedé sin sentido. | I passed out. |
| Primero tienes que atravesar un cruce. | First, you have to pass through an intersection. |
| No dejes pasar esta oportunidad. | Don't pass up this opportunity. |
| Dejé el colegio a los 15 años. | I dropped out of school when I was 15. |
| Nos quedamos levantados hasta las tantas. | We stayed up very late. |
| Nos quedamos por ahí hasta las tantas. | We stayed out very late. |
| Le gusta presumir. | He likes to show off. |
| No sé cómo transmitírselo. | I don't know how to get it across to them. |

**Key notes:**

- **pass by** = *pasar por* a place briefly on your way somewhere. **drop by** works too: *I'll drop by your house on the way to mine.*
- **pass away** = *fallecer* (a polite way to say *to die*). Informal/humorous: **to kick the bucket**.
- **a crossroads / an intersection** = *un cruce (de calles)*.
- **a los 15 años** → **when I was 15 (years old)**.
- **No sé cómo transmitírselo** was the "10 bonus points" sentence: see Section 2 for the word order.

sections.title: 2. Phrasal Verbs Review: Pass, Drop Out, Stay, Show Off, Get Across
sections.content:
### Pass + particle

| Phrasal verb | Spanish | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **pass by** | pasar por (brevemente) | I'll pass by your house on the way to mine. |
| **pass away** | fallecer | The good lady passed away after a long illness. |
| **pass out** (1) | desmayarse, quedarse sin sentido | I passed out. (= I fainted / I lost consciousness) |
| **pass out** (2) | repartir, distribuir | The teacher passed out the exams. *(see Sep 29: Out = distributing)* |
| **pass through** | atravesar | First, you have to pass through an intersection. |
| **pass up** | dejar pasar (una oportunidad) | Don't pass up this opportunity. |

### Conscious vs. Aware

- After you **pass out** you are **unconscious**; when you wake up, the doctor says *He's conscious* (= awake).
- *Ser consciente de algo* is normally **to be aware of** something, not ~~to be conscious of~~:
  - *Were you aware of the fact that a lot of people are dealing with stress these days?*

### Drop out of vs. Give up

- **drop out (of)** = stop being a member / discontinue (*dejar* a school, club, course): *I used to do karate, but I dropped out when I was 10.*
- **give up** = *dejar* a habit: *I gave up smoking.*
- **quit** covers both: *I quit school.*

### Stay up vs. Stay out

- **stay up (late)** = *quedarse levantado / despierto*, usually at home.
- **stay out (late)** = *quedarse por ahí*, away from home.
- *Last Saturday I didn't stay out long. I came home early, but I stayed up late watching a movie.*

### Show off

- **show off** = *presumir, fardar*: *He likes to show off.*

### Get (something) across (to someone)

- **get across** = *transmitir* an idea, information or a message. Don't use *transmit*: that's for signals (a radio transmitter).
- It's **separable**, and with pronouns the order is **get + it + across + to + them**, the same pattern as *She baked **it for us*** or *I did **it for you***:
  - ✅ **I don't know how to get it across to them.**
  - ❌ ~~I don't know how to get it them across~~ · ❌ ~~get across it~~
- *He's good at getting his point across.*

sections.title: 3. Reading: Red Cloud
sections.content:
Kyle read his own short text about **Red Cloud** (born 1822), a war leader of the Oglala Lakota (Sioux). Kyle says he's less famous than Geronimo, Sitting Bull or Crazy Horse, but he's Kyle's favourite.

**The story in brief:**

- **The Bozeman Trail.** In the 1860s, gold was found in Montana. Miners and settlers began crossing the Powder River Country, which was Lakota and Cheyenne hunting ground protected by treaty. The US Army built a string of forts along the trail to protect them.
- **Red Cloud's War (1866–1868).** Red Cloud treated the forts as a violation of sovereignty and fought a guerrilla campaign. In the **Fetterman Fight** (1866), warriors **lured** a detachment of 81 soldiers into a trap and **wiped** them **out**. The trail became unusable for over a year.
- **The Treaty of Fort Laramie (1868).** The US government **admitted defeat**. It agreed to abandon the forts, close the trail to settlers, and create the Great Sioux Reservation, securing the Black Hills for Native occupancy. Red Cloud is remembered as the only Native American leader to win a major war against the United States.
- **Inspiration to Sitting Bull.** Younger leaders like Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse fought alongside him. He showed a new generation of **Plains** warriors that the US Army was not invincible.

**From the discussion:**

- There were **no railways** in Montana in the 1860s (they came in the 1870s), so the **trail** was a route for horses and wagons, a *camino*.
- **the gold rush** = *la fiebre del oro*: literally everyone *rushing* (going *con prisa*) to California, or later to the Klondike (Yukon and Alaska).
- Today we say **Native American** rather than *Indian*.
- Kyle mentioned Canada's **National Day of Truth and Reconciliation** (Sep 30), and a student recommended *Bury My Heart at Wounded Knee* as a film about Sitting Bull. A Sitting Bull reading may come next.

> The class answers: *life experiences*, *education*, *family and education* — they're all connected!

sections.title: 2. Siblings — Brothers, Sisters or Siblings?
sections.content:
**Siblings** = brothers and sisters (*hermanos*, without specifying gender).

| You have… | You say… |
|---|---|
| two boys | *I have two **brothers**.* (only male) |
| two girls | *I have two **sisters**.* (only female) |
| one boy and one girl | *I have two **siblings**.* / *I have a brother and a sister.* |
| no brothers or sisters | *I'm an **only child**.* |

**Birth order:** the **oldest** / **eldest** child · the **middle** child · the **youngest** child

💡 Use *siblings* when you don't want to specify the gender — e.g. *Why older **siblings** are more likely to be successful.*

sections.title: 3. Reading — Why Older Siblings Are More Likely To Be Successful (Part 1)
sections.content:
*Adapted from The Telegraph.*

> "I'm the oldest child. I make the rules," read a **mug** my family owned when I was small. "I'm the middle child. I am the reason there are rules." And then underneath, "I am the youngest child. I'm above the rules."
>
> We have lots of **preconceptions** about what the **birth order** of siblings means, and that mug seemed perfectly **accurate** to me: the responsible, **ambitious** eldest child, the middle child who is difficult to deal with, and the **easy-going** youngest. But what does this birth order mean when siblings grow up? Yes, people think that elder siblings are more ambitious, but is that really so, and does it mean that they **earn** more?
>
> We know that a person's parents, **spouse** and children all have significant effects on how **wealthy** they may become, but the **impact** of siblings is not so easy to see.

---

- **Mug** = a big cup (*taza*), the kind you use for *café con leche*.
- **To earn** = to make money (*ganar dinero*).

📖 **Reading tip:** read once for the general idea (*scanning*), read again for the details, then **summarise** it in your own words.

sections.title: 4. Vocabulary — Find the Word in the Text
sections.content:
| Meaning | Word from the text |
|---|---|
| Correct and true | **accurate** |
| Very motivated | **ambitious** |
| Relaxed and not worried about things | **easy-going** (don't forget the hyphen!) |
| Husband or wife | **spouse** (*cónyuge*) — pronounced *spouse*, no "e" sound at the end |
| Having a lot of money, rich | **wealthy** (W-E-A-L-T-H-Y) |
| A strong effect | **impact** |

---

### Fill in the gaps

| Sentence | Answer |
|---|---|
| Even as a child, my brother was very ___ and always wanted to be the best student in his class. | **ambitious** |
| I have a good relationship with my ___'s brother and sister. We often spend time together. | **spouse** |
| I grew up with two ___, an older sister and a younger brother, and we used to argue a lot. | **siblings** |
| My sister is quite ___. Even when things go wrong, she stays calm and doesn't panic. | **easy-going** |
| My aunt and uncle became quite ___ after starting their own business, but they still live a very simple life. | **wealthy** |
| My older sister had a big ___ on me because she encouraged me to study English and travel more. | **impact** |
| My granddad told me amazing stories about his travels, but now I'm not sure how ___ they were. | **accurate** |

💡 You always have an impact **on** something: *She had a big impact **on** me.*

sections.title: 5. Translation Practice
sections.content:

| La familia es muy rica, pero vive de forma bastante sencilla. | The family is very **wealthy**, but **they** live quite **simply**. |
| Ese profesor cambió mi vida más de lo que imagina. | That teacher had a bigger **impact on** my life than he **realises**. |

⚠️ **Watch out!**
- *Buscamos* = an action happening now → **present continuous**: *We're looking for…*
- *Surprisingly* is an **adverb** (how it was) → add **-ly**.
- *The family* is singular, but the people in it live simply → **they** live.
- *Simply* or *in a simple way* — don't mix the two.

title: Brain Buffet
topic: Reading! — Siblings and Success (Part 2)

sections.title: 1. Review — Siblings and Success (Part 1)
sections.content:
This class continues the article *"Why Older Siblings Are More Likely To Be Successful"* (see the Jul 9 class).

- **Siblings** = brothers and sisters (*hermanos*), when you don't specify the gender.
- Vocabulary from Part 1: **accurate** · **ambitious** · **easy-going** · **spouse** · **wealthy** · **impact**

sections.title: 2. Reading Skill — What Does "this" Refer To?
sections.content:
The pronoun **this** usually refers back to something **already mentioned** in the text, often close to it. Training your brain to find it is key for understanding articles, books and proficiency exams.

> Research has found that older siblings often have higher IQs than younger siblings, and **this** (1) does lead to higher earnings on average, some data suggest. Research in 2021, analysing data from Denmark in the 1980s, found that older siblings earned about 2.4% more than younger ones. Researchers said that **this** (2) was because younger siblings were more likely to spend time in hospital as small children, and that **this** (3) had a negative effect on them throughout school and their early working lives. But **this** (4) doesn't tell the whole story, and it doesn't reflect what siblings themselves say about the impact they have had on each other's lives and earnings.

| "this" | refers to… |
|---|---|
| (1) | the fact that older siblings have **higher IQs** than younger siblings |
| (2) | the **2.4% salary difference** (not the hospital stays!) |
| (3) | the fact that younger siblings **spent more time in hospital** |
| (4) | the **explanation** that older siblings earn more |

sections.title: 3. Reading — Siblings Can Push Each Other to Achieve
sections.content:
🧠 **Before reading:** how do you think the relationship between two siblings, Divya and Aditya, who moved from India to the UK, impacted each other's professional success?

> Aditya Anandkumar decided to move to the UK from India four years ago to go to university, partly because his eldest sister, Divya, had done it too. She started a master's in economics in 2021 at the University of Glasgow and later earned a PhD in game theory.
>
> *"The fact that my sister was already in the UK made me realise that it was possible to go. Once someone in your family is already there, it's not a dream anymore,"* he says. *"Looking at Divya, I get inspiration from her."*
>
> Aditya, 24, and Divya, 31, now both work in London and live together. He's a financial reporter and she works for Amazon, and they earn about the same amount. Divya is slightly ahead in earnings if company shares are included.
>
> Divya says that being the eldest meant she spoke more to their parents about their finances, and that this encouraged her to earn well. Now the siblings support each other with career advice. Aditya says that he was lazier at school than Divya, but with time, his results got even better than hers.
>
> Siblings pushing each other in this way is called the **sibling spillover effect**. Emma Zeng, an academic at Yale University, says: *"We found that having an academically successful older sibling positively affects the younger sibling's academic performance. He or she could be a very good **role model**."*

💬 **The class's views:** it depends on personality and environment too · they have a good **rapport** and help each other · but the success of one can also have a *negative* effect on the other if the difference is big.

sections.title: 4. True or False? + The Sibling Spillover Effect
sections.content:
| Statement | |
|---|---|
| The younger brother moved to the UK first. | ❌ False — Divya (the older sister) went first |
| The siblings chose similar careers. | ❌ False — he's a financial reporter, she works for Amazon |
| The sister makes more money. | ✅ True — slightly, if company shares are included |
| The sister wanted to earn well because she had a rich friend. | ❌ False — conversations with her parents about finances encouraged her |
| The sibling spillover effect is when one sibling's behaviour has a positive impact on the other. | ✅ True |

---

**Spillover** = *derrame* (from *to spill* = *derramar, verter*). Imagine a glass of water that overflows: everything around it gets wet. In the **sibling spillover effect**, the "water" is something **positive** — one sibling's success *spills over* and influences the siblings around them.

sections.title: 5. Translation Practice
sections.content:
| Español | English |
|---|---|
| Mis hermanos siempre me ayudan cuando los necesito. | My **siblings** always help me when I need them. |
| El informe no era del todo preciso. | The report wasn't **completely** / **entirely accurate**. |
| A pesar de ser rico, lleva una vida sencilla. | **Despite being wealthy**, he lives a simple life. |

💡 After **despite**, use the **-ing** form: *despite being…* — or *despite the fact that he's wealthy*.

'El informe no era del todo preciso.'

title: Brain Buffet
topic: Articles — Hot Take

sections.title: 1. Discussion — Hot Takes
sections.content:
A **hot take** = an **unpopular opinion** (*opinión polémica*): a controversial statement, often shared on social media, that goes against the mainstream.

Do you agree or disagree?

| | Hot take |
|---|---|
| 🔇 | Silence is better than music. |
| 🥣 | Milk ruins cereal. |
| 👶 | Parenting should require a licence. |
| 💰 | Money can buy happiness. |
| 🎭 | Shakespeare wasn't that great. |

> *"Silence is part of the music too."* · *"Money can't always buy happiness, but it helps."*

sections.title: 2. Articles — The Three Basic Rules
sections.content:
**Definite article:** *the* · **Indefinite articles:** *a / an*. The same word can need *the*, *a* or **no article** — it depends on the context.

| Sentence | Why? |
|---|---|
| *Bye, Dad, I'm going to **school**.* | school as an **institution** → no article |
| *I'm at **the** school waiting for you.* | a school **both speakers know** |
| *Look, Mummy, I think that's **the** moon.* | there's **only one** (our Moon) |
| *Look at that tiny dot next to the planet. I think that's **a** moon.* | **naming** something |
| ***The** bear's diet consists of roots, berries and insects.* | singular noun for things **in general** |
| *See that cave? **A** bear lives there.* | **non-specific**, mentioned for the first time |
| ***Children** love playing.* | **in general** → no article |
| ***The** children love playing in the living room.* | **specific** children |

---

### A. No article
- Things **in general** (plurals and uncountable nouns): *Games are popular among teenagers.* · *Grammar is hard.*
- Someone is part of an **institution**: *They are in hospital.* · *She went to prison.* · *I'm going to school.*

### B. Indefinite article (a / an)
- **Naming** things: *This is a glass.* · *I think that's a moon.*
- Mentioning something **for the first time** or **non-specific**: *I found a brick.* · *A bear lives there.*

### C. Definite article (the)
- Something **mentioned before** or that **both speakers understand**: *Have you seen the file?*
- When there is **only one**: *The sky is blue.* · *The moon is our satellite.*
- With **adjectives** and **singular nouns** for things **in general**: *I work with the elderly.* · *The compass has been used for thousands of years.*

⚠️ *Compass has been used…* ❌ → ***The** compass has been used…* ✅ or ***Compasses** have been used…* ✅

sections.title: 3. Reading — Articles in Context
sections.content:
> Do you remember **the woman that I talked to yesterday**? She might be **the nicest** person I've ever met. She's **an architect** at my company. She joined the firm in **the 2010s**, and before that, she had worked in **Peru** and in **the UK**. Yesterday, I asked her to give me some advice on professional development, and she invited me for **lunch**. She said that it would give us more time to talk. So today, we're **taking a break** at 1:00, and we're going to that nice restaurant **round the corner**. I'm going to ask her about **the benefits of** working for architecture firms abroad. I'm hoping to get some sound professional advice **at last**.

| Rule | Example from the text |
|---|---|
| **No article** with **meals** | *for **lunch*** · *coffee for breakfast* |
| **No article** with most **place names** (cities, countries, continents) | *in **Peru*** · *in France* · *in Madrid* |
| **The** with **defining relative clauses** (extra info that tells you *which* one) | ***the** woman that I talked to yesterday* |
| **The** with **superlatives** | ***the** nicest person* · *the best* · *the most intelligent* |
| **The** with **decades and centuries** | ***the** 2010s* · *the '90s* |
| **The** with countries with **plural nouns or political terms**, and rivers, mountain ranges, oceans, seas, deserts | ***the** UK* · *the USA* · *the EU* · *the United States* |
| **The** with something **defined by *of*** | ***the** benefits of working…* |
| **Fixed expressions** (just learn them!) | *take **a** break* · *round **the** corner* · *at last* |
| **A / an** when naming someone's **profession** | *She's **an** architect.* · *I'm **a** teacher.* |

💡 New expression: **to hit the ground running** = to start something with energy and at full speed.

title: Brain Buffet
topic: Past Modal Verbs and Idioms

sections.title: 1. Idioms for Emotions — Complete the Dialogues
sections.content:
Words in the box: **air · dumps · feet · leaf · pink · thunder**

| Dialogue | Answer |
|---|---|
| A: *Mike has just finished a meeting with his boss, and he has a face like ___.* B: *He might have been fired or something.* A: *He can't have been fired because he was promoted last week.* | **thunder** |
| A: *Why aren't you walking on ___? The exams are over.* B: *Yeah, I know, but I might not have passed one of them.* | **air** |
| A: *She was dead on her ___ and fell asleep right after she came home.* B: *She must have had a night shift this week. They're very exhausting.* | **feet** |
| A: *What's wrong with him? He's shaking like a ___.* B: *He may have seen a ghost.* A: *Oh, come on, he couldn't have seen a ghost. Ghosts don't exist.* | **leaf** |
| A: *Alex broke off her engagement to Max six months ago.* B: *Really? What happened?* A: *I think he could have cheated on her.* B: *She must have felt down in the ___. Poor thing.* | **dumps** |
| A: *Frank is going to the Royal Gala Night this year.* B: *He must have been tickled ___ to get the invitation. He loves posh parties like that.* | **pink** |

sections.title: 2. What Do the Idioms Mean?
sections.content:
| Idiom | Emotion | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **to have a face like thunder** | 😠 anger | to look very angry |
| **to be walking on air** | 🤩 euphoria | to be extremely happy (and relieved) |
| **to be dead on your feet** | 😴 tiredness | to be exhausted |
| **to be shaking like a leaf** | 😨 fear | to tremble because you're scared (not cold!) |
| **to feel down in the dumps** | 😢 sadness | to feel very low, depressed |
| **to be tickled pink** | 😊 delight | to be delighted — old-fashioned, rarely used today |

💡 Bonus expressions from the class: **sooner rather than later** · **to be on the ball** (to be quick to react).

sections.title: 3. Translation Practice — Idioms
sections.content:
| Español | English |
|---|---|
| Después de la reunión, él tenía una cara de pocos amigos. | After the meeting, he had **a face like thunder**. |
| Después de recibir la noticia, ella estaba en una nube. | After **hearing** the news, she was **walking on air**. |
| Antes del examen, él temblaba como una hoja. | Before the exam, he was **shaking like a leaf**. |

⚠️ With *news* we use **hear**, not *receive*: *after **hearing** the news*.

sections.title: 4. Grammar — Past Modals of Deduction
sections.content:
We use **modal + have + past participle** to make **deductions and guesses about the past** — things we're not 100% sure about.

| How sure? | Modal | Example |
|---|---|---|
| ✅ **Almost sure it's true** (very likely) | **must have** | *She **must have had** a night shift.* |
| 🤔 **Less sure — possible** | **might / may / could have** | *He **might have been** fired.* · *He **may have seen** a ghost.* · *He **could have cheated** on her.* |
| ❌ **Almost sure it's NOT true** (very unlikely / impossible) | **can't / couldn't have** | *He **can't have been** fired.* · *He **couldn't have seen** a ghost.* |

Negative possibility: *I **might not have passed** one of them.*

⚠️ **Have** is always there — but not *have had*! Use *have had* only when the main verb is *have*:
- *She must **have had** a good time.* (verb: *have* a good time)
- *He might **have committed** a crime.* ✅ — not ~~*have had committed*~~

And always the **past participle** (third column): *must have **paid*** ✅ — not ~~*must have pay*~~.

sections.title: 5. Practice — React to the Situation
sections.content:
| Situation | Clue | Reaction |
|---|---|---|
| Julie spent the weekend hiking with her best friend. | *must / have a good time* | She **must have had** a good time. |
| Your son is at the police station. | *might / commit a crime* | He **might have committed** a crime. |
| She saw her driving to work yesterday. | *can't / see her* | She **can't have seen** her. She's been out of town for the past week. |
| They booked a luxury trip to the Caribbean. | *must / pay a lot of money* | They **must have paid** a lot of money. |

'She was dead on her ___ and fell asleep right after she came home.'

'She must have felt down in the dumps.' How did she feel?
'He must have been tickled pink to get the invitation.' How did he feel?
'Después de recibir la noticia, ella estaba en una nube.'

After hearing the news, she was walking on air.
After hearing the news, she was dead on her feet.
After listening the news, she was in a cloud.
qs.ans: After hearing the news, she was walking on air.
