Julie spent the weekend hiking with her best friend. → She ___ a good time.
Your son is at the police station. → He ___ a crime.
They booked a luxury trip to the Caribbean. → They ___ a lot of money.
'He couldn't have seen a ghost. Ghosts don't exist.' How sure is the speaker?

He's almost sure he saw one
qs.ans: He's almost sure he didn't see one

sections.title: 3. Synonyms — Which Is Stronger?
sections.content:
| Gradable (weaker) | Ungradable (extreme) |
|---|---|
| bad | **awful** |
| hungry | **starving** |
| angry | **furious** |
| tired | **exhausted** |

| scared | **terrified** |
| dirty | **filthy** |

sections.title: 4. Grammar — Gradable vs. Ungradable Adjectives
sections.content:
- **Gradable** adjectives (*angry, bad, dirty*) have a **weaker** meaning than **ungradable** adjectives (*terrified, awful, filthy*).
- **Ungradable** adjectives are **not** used in comparative and superlative forms, because their meaning is already **extreme**. You can be *more tired* than someone, but not ~~*more exhausted*~~.

| Before **gradable** adjectives (tell the *degree*) | Before **ungradable** adjectives (only *emphasise*) |
|---|---|
| **quite · a bit · very · really** | **completely · absolutely · really** |
| *I was **a bit** / **quite** / **very** angry.* | *I was **absolutely** / **completely** furious.* |

⭐ **Really** works with **both**: *really angry* ✅ · *really furious* ✅

❌ ~~*very terrified*~~ · ~~*a bit exhausted*~~ · ~~*quite filthy*~~ — *terrified* is already the top level of fear: there are no degrees.

sections.title: 5. Practice — Choose the Right Word
sections.content:
**A.** Akane had been driving for eight hours to visit her parents, and she was **completely** *(completely / very)* exhausted. When she got to their home, she discovered they were not there and was **quite scared** *(scared / terrified)*. When she called them, they told her that they had forgotten she was coming and had gone away for the weekend. They felt **absolutely** *(a bit / absolutely)* awful.

**B.** Monica had been working hard, hoping to get a promotion. One day, her boss called her into the office, and she was excited for the good news. However, she was **very** *(very / completely)* sad when her boss asked her to sign a card for her colleague Diego, who had just received the promotion instead. Monica thought that Diego was **a bit** *(a bit / absolutely)* lazy. She felt **really angry / really furious** — ✅ **both**, because *really* goes with both!

**C.** Aziz let his brother Abdul stay in his flat after he lost his job. One evening, when Aziz went out, Abdul invited his friends over. They were **absolutely / really starving** — ✅ **both** — so they made pasta for dinner. When Aziz returned home, the kitchen was very **dirty** *(dirty / filthy)*, as Abdul had not cleaned up his mess.

qs.q: What is the extreme (ungradable) form of 'hungry'?
What is the extreme (ungradable) form of 'dirty'?
What is the extreme (ungradable) form of 'sad'?
What is the extreme (ungradable) form of 'scared'?
What is the extreme (ungradable) form of 'angry'?
What is the extreme (ungradable) form of 'tired'?
What does 'filthy' mean?
'After driving for eight hours, she was ___ exhausted.'
'She discovered they were not there and was quite ___.'
'They felt ___ awful.'
'She was ___ sad when her boss asked her to sign the card.'
'When Aziz returned home, the kitchen was very ___.'
Which intensifier can be used with BOTH gradable and ungradable adjectives?
Which sentence is correct?
opts: I'm very terrified of big dogs.
I'm absolutely terrified of big dogs.
I'm a bit terrified of big dogs.
I'm quite terrified of big dogs.
qs.ans: I'm absolutely terrified of big dogs.

qs.q: Why can't we say 'more exhausted than'?
opts: Exhausted is already extreme, so it has no degrees
Exhausted is only used in the past
qs.ans: Exhausted is already extreme, so it has no degrees

title: Natural English
topic: To Be Worth + -ing / To Make It

sections.title: 1. Two Natural Upgrades
sections.content:
Two structures that **replace** things we already know with a more natural, native option. Neither version is wrong — these just **elevate** your English:

- *The film is good.* → *The film **is worth watching**.*
- *We arrived.* → *We **made it**.*

sections.title: 2. To Be Worth + -ing
sections.content:
**Formula:** subject + **be** + **worth** + **verb-ing** (the action you do with that thing) = *merece la pena + verbo*.

A film is *watched*, a book is *read*, a museum is *visited* — pick the verb that matches the thing.

| Standard | Natural |
|---|---|
| It is good to try that restaurant. | That restaurant **is worth trying**. |
| I really recommend reading that book. | That book **is worth reading**. |
| It is a good idea to visit the new museum. | The new museum **is worth visiting**. |
| I highly recommend that you download this app. | This app **is worth downloading**. |
| It is a good idea to watch that series. | That series **is worth watching**. |
| I recommend that you check out that coffee shop. | That coffee shop **is worth checking out**. |
| It is a good idea to take this course. | This course **is worth taking**. |
| I recommend that you buy a plasma TV. | A plasma TV **is worth buying**. |

### With *it* (the subject is understood from context)

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Is it worth going? | Yes, **it's worth going**. |
| Is it worth paying extra? | Yes, **it's worth paying extra**. |
| Is it worth studying abroad? | Yes, **it's worth studying abroad**. |
| Are they worth investing your time? | Yes, **they are worth investing** your time. |

### With a noun
- *Rome is **a city worth visiting**.*
- *Hamlet is **a book worth reading**.*
- *Exercise is **a habit worth developing**.*
- *My boss **isn't worth worrying about**.*

sections.title: 3. To Make It = To Arrive / Get There
sections.content:
Besides **arrive** and **get**, natives constantly use **make it** (*llegar, conseguir llegar*). It's a **pack** — always *make + it* together. Add **to** before the destination (like *get to*).

| Standard | Natural |
|---|---|
| The traffic was terrible, but we arrived. | The traffic was terrible, but we **made it**. |
| I'm sorry, I can't arrive. | I'm sorry, I **can't make it**. |
| Do you think you will arrive on time? | Do you think you'll **make it** on time? |
| We got to London in the end. | We **made it to** London in the end. |
| Did you get to the meeting? | Did you **make it to** the meeting? |
| We arrived at the airport. | We **made it to** the airport. |
| I got home. | I **made it home**. |

**Q&A:** *Did you make it to your flight?* — *Yes, I made it.* · *Can you make it to my party?* — *No, I can't make it.* · *Did they make it to the finish line?* — *Yes, they made it.*

💡 *home* takes no *to*: *I made it **home***.

qs.q: 'I really recommend reading that book.' → Natural version:
opts: That book is worth to read.

qs.q: 'It is a good idea to visit the new museum.' → Natural version:
opts: The new museum is worth visiting.
The new museum is worth to visit.
It worth visiting the new museum.
The new museum is worthy visit.
qs.ans: The new museum is worth visiting.

qs.q: 'Is it worth paying extra?' — positive answer:
opts: Yes, it's worth to pay extra.

qs.q: What form does the verb take after 'worth'?
'I'm sorry, I can't arrive.' → Natural version:
opts: I'm sorry, I can't make it.
I'm sorry, I can't do it.
I'm sorry, I can't make there.
qs.ans: I'm sorry, I can't make it.

qs.q: 'We got to London in the end.' → Natural version:
opts: We made it London in the end.
We made it to London in the end.
We made to London in the end.
We made London in the end.
qs.ans: We made it to London in the end.

qs.q: 'I got home.' → Natural version:
'My boss isn't ___ about.'

title: Natural English
topic: Keeping the Flow in a Conversation

sections.title: 1. Why Follow-Up Questions Matter
sections.content:
Without the right resources, a conversation becomes *question, answer, question, answer* — robotic and artificial. **Follow-up questions** ask for more details about whatever the other person just said, and they work in **any** conversation.

💡 Avoid answering with a bare question word (*Why? How?*). A fuller follow-up shows you're listening and connects you with the speaker.

sections.title: 2. How Come…? (¿Cómo es que…?)
sections.content:
**How come** + the sentence exactly as it is — **no question inversion**, any tense, positive or negative.

| They say… | You ask… |
|---|---|
| I'm not working at the moment. | **How come** you're not working at the moment? |
| I've changed jobs. | **How come** you've changed jobs? |
| My mom's learning Italian. | **How come** your mom's learning Italian? |
| I moved last month. | **How come** you moved last month? |
| My boss was angry at me. | **How come** your boss was angry at you? |

⚠️ *cambiar de trabajo* = **change jobs** (plural, no *of*).

💡 Don't confuse it with **How about…?**, which makes a suggestion: *How about Friday?*

sections.title: 3. How Was It? / What Was It Like?
sections.content:
To ask for someone's **opinion or experience** (*¿Y cómo fue?*) — not *what happened*, but *what was it like for you*.

| They say… | You ask… |
|---|---|
| I travelled to Italy last year. | And **how was it**? / And **what was it like**? |
| The performance was at 8. | And how was it? / And what was it like? |
| My boss asked me to make a speech. | And how was it? / And what was it like? |

💡 Use **it** — *And how was the speech?* repeats the noun and sounds redundant.

sections.title: 4. And Then What? / How Did You End Up…?
sections.content:
**And then what?** (*¿Y luego qué?*) — to make the story continue: *I found a ring in the street.* — *And then what?*

**How did you end up + -ing / place?** (*¿Cómo acabaste…?*) — when they tell you the **end** of the story and you want the rest. Use **end up**, not *finish*.

| They say… | You ask… |
|---|---|
| I moved to the other side of the world. | And how did you **end up moving** to the other side of the world? |
| In the end, I was alone in the middle of the road. | And how did you **end up** alone in the middle of the road? |
| She went to a different doctor. | And how did she **end up going** to a different doctor? |
| I was by myself on the plane. | And how did you **end up** by yourself on the plane? |

🎭 Tone matters: an excited *And then what?* shows curiosity; a flat *Yeah… and then what?* sounds sceptical.

sections.title: 5. How So? / In What Way?
sections.content:
To ask for **more elaboration** (*¿De qué manera?*). **How so?** is used **alone** — *so* replaces everything they said.

| They say… | You ask… |
|---|---|
| It was one of the hardest jobs I've ever done. | **How so?** / **In what way?** |
| I absolutely loved living in that country. | How so? / In what way? |
| I offered to help him. | How so? / In what way? |

📝 **Practice:** imagine conversations and react out loud — *And how come you didn't call me? · And how come the window is broken?*

qs.q: 'I've changed jobs.' → Natural follow-up:
opts: How come did you change jobs?
How come have you changed jobs?

qs.q: Which statement about 'how come' is true?
opts: It needs an auxiliary and inversion
The sentence keeps normal word order
It only works in the present
qs.ans: The sentence keeps normal word order

qs.q: 'I travelled to Italy last year.' → Ask for their experience:
'My boss asked me to make a speech.' Which follow-up sounds most natural?
opts: And how was the speech it?

qs.q: 'I found a ring in the street.' → Make the story continue:
'I moved to the other side of the world.' → Ask how that happened:
opts: How did you finish moving there?
How did you end up moving to the other side of the world?
How did you end moving to the other side of the world?
How did you end up to move there?
qs.ans: How did you end up moving to the other side of the world?

qs.q: 'It was one of the hardest jobs I've ever done.' → Ask for more elaboration:
What is 'cambiar de trabajo' in English?

title: Natural English
topic: Saying More with Fewer Words

sections.title: 1. Be Efficient
sections.content: In Spanish, long sentences and complex structures can sound impressive. In **spoken English** it's the opposite: good speakers say things with **as few words as possible**. Going too far sounds artificial.

sections.title: 2. Dropping the Subject
sections.content:
Books say English always needs a subject (there are no verb endings to tell you who it is). But in conversation, when you talk about **yourself**, you can drop the **subject + auxiliary** pack.

| Full sentence | Natural |
|---|---|
| I'm not sure. | **Not sure.** |
| It's nice to meet you. | **Nice to meet you.** |
| I'm glad you came. | **Glad you came.** |
| I'm happy to be here. | **Happy to be here.** |
| I've never been here. | **Never been here.** |
| I'm sorry I'm late. | **Sorry I'm late.** |
| It's nice to see you. | **Nice to see you.** |
| I'm happy to help. | **Happy to help.** |
| I've never tried it. | **Never tried it.** |
| I'm looking forward to it. | **Looking forward to it.** |

💡 Very common with feelings and opinions (*glad, happy, sorry*) — it's obvious you mean yourself.

sections.title: 3. No + Noun
sections.content:
Replace a long negative sentence with **no + noun**. Always **no**, never *not*.

| Long version | Short version | Español |
|---|---|---|
| I don't have any idea. | **No idea.** | No tengo ni idea |
| It isn't a problem. | **No problem.** | No hay problema |
| Don't worry about it. | **No worries.** (plural!) | No pasa nada |
| There isn't a chance. | **No chance.** | Ni hablar / imposible |
| There isn't a way. | **No way.** | De ninguna manera |
| I don't wonder why. | **No wonder.** | No me extraña |
| We don't need to rush. | **No rush.** | No hay prisa |
| There isn't a doubt. | **No doubt.** | Sin duda |
| There isn't a point. | **No point.** | No merece la pena |

### Extend them with more information
- *I don't know what to say.* → ***No idea** what to say.*
- *I don't wonder why he's sad.* → ***No wonder** he's sad.*
- *It's impossible that he's the new boss.* → ***No chance** he's the new boss.*
- *Take your time doing this.* → ***No rush** doing this.*
- *There isn't a way that this is correct.* → ***No way** this is correct.*

sections.title: 4. Short Natural Shortcuts
sections.content:
| Meaning | Shortcut | Español |
|---|---|---|
| That's okay with me. | **Works for me.** | Me vale |
| I understand your point. | **Fair enough.** | Pues sí, lo veo |
| It was my mistake. | **My bad.** | Culpa mía |
| You can make the decision. | **Up to you.** / **Your call.** | Tú verás / cosa tuya |
| That was a smart decision. | **Good call.** | Bien hecho, buena decisión |

💡 *I see* only shows you're listening; **fair enough** shows you actually accept their point.

qs.q: 'I've never been here.' → Shorter, natural version:
When can you drop the subject in conversation?
'Don't worry about it.' → Short version:
'Take your time.' → Short version:
'It's useless.' → Short version:
'I don't wonder why he's sad.' → Short version:
How do you say 'Me vale' (that's okay with me)?
How do you say 'Culpa mía'?
Which two shortcuts mean 'you can make the decision'?

title: Natural English
topic: Avoiding Speaking in Absolutes

sections.title: 1. Why Avoid Absolutes?
sections.content:
Absolute words — **always, never, everyone, no one, impossible, perfect** — are the top level of each message. In English, very definite statements sound **intense** or **blunt**. Natives prefer to be more **nuanced** (*matizado*): the message is the same, but it sounds softer and more appropriate.

> It's basically *hablar sin mojarse*.

sections.title: 2. Softer Alternatives
sections.content:
| Absolute | Softer | Example |
|---|---|---|
| impossible | **unlikely** (*poco probable*) | *It's **unlikely** that you're ready at eight.* |
| everybody / everyone | **most people** / **lots of people** | ***Most people** do that.* |
| nobody / no one | **few people** / **very few people** | ***Very few people** like war.* |
| never | **rarely** (best) / **hardly ever** | *I **rarely** make good decisions.* |
| always | **often** / almost always | *She **often** calls me in the morning.* |
| He's rude. | **seem + a bit** | *He **seems a bit** rude.* |

⚠️ *casi nunca* = **hardly ever**, not ~~*almost never*~~ or ~~*rarely ever*~~.

💡 **seem** = it's my impression (maybe not the full truth) · **a bit** softens the adjective.

sections.title: 3. Not Exactly / Not Necessarily
sections.content:
Put **exactly** or **necessarily** in the middle to soften a negative (*no es exactamente / necesariamente…*).

🗣️ **exactly** — drop the *t*: *exac-ly* · **necessarily** — *NE-ce-sa-ri-ly*

| Blunt | Softer |
|---|---|
| It isn't cheap. | It isn't **exactly** / **necessarily** cheap. |
| You're not right. | You're not **exactly** right. |
| That wasn't true. | That wasn't **necessarily** true. |
| Knowing grammar doesn't mean that you can speak English. | Knowing grammar doesn't **necessarily** mean that you can speak English. |
| Working long hours won't help your career. | Working long hours won't **exactly** help your career. |

sections.title: 4. Practice — Take the Intensity Out
sections.content:
| Absolute | Softer |
|---|---|
| Everybody thinks I'm crazy. | **Most people** think I'm crazy. |
| My boss never tells me off. | My boss **rarely** tells me off. |
| Nobody's going to help me. | **Very few people** are going to help me. |
| It's impossible that she's your cousin. | It's **unlikely** that she's your cousin. |
| The new manager is unpleasant. | The new manager **seems a bit** unpleasant. |
| My friends are always there when I need them. | My friends are **often** there when I need them. |
| Liking music doesn't mean that you can dance. | Liking music doesn't **necessarily** mean that you can dance. |
| Your dog is scary. | Your dog **seems a bit** scary. |

📖 **tell someone off** = *regañar, echar la bronca* · **fearful** = *miedoso* (always scared) vs. **scared** = *asustado* (right now) · **scary** = *que da miedo*

qs.q: Softer alternative to 'impossible':
'Everybody does that.' → Softer:
'Nobody likes war.' → Softer:
How do you say 'casi nunca'?
'He's rude.' → Softer:
'She always calls me in the morning.' → Softer:
opts: She often calls me in the morning.
She rarely calls me in the morning.
She hardly calls me in the morning.
She never calls me in the morning.
qs.ans: She often calls me in the morning.

qs.q: 'Knowing grammar doesn't mean you can speak English.' → Softer:
opts: Knowing grammar doesn't necessarily mean you can speak English.
Knowing grammar necessarily doesn't mean you can speak English.
Knowing grammar doesn't mean necessary you can speak English.
Knowing grammar doesn't exact mean you can speak English.
qs.ans: Knowing grammar doesn't necessarily mean you can speak English.

qs.q: What does 'to tell someone off' mean?

title: Natural English
topic: Self-Correcting

sections.title: 1. Mistakes Are Human
sections.content:
We all say the wrong thing sometimes — *I saw him on Wednesday… no, Thursday*. Instead of trying to be perfect, learn **how to manage mistakes** naturally. People who correct themselves smoothly sound **more** natural than people who never slip.

🎭 Use natural intonation, like in Spanish: *Fui a Italia el año pasado… espera, no, fue el anterior.*

sections.title: 2. Correcting Facts
sections.content:
| Connector | Example |
|---|---|
| **Actually** / **Actually, no** | *I started learning English when I was 12. **Actually**, I was 11.* |
|  | *I've worked in this company for six years. **Actually, no**, seven.* |
| **No, wait** (*No, espera*) | *We stayed at the hotel for five days. **No, wait**, it was six.* |
|  | *She lives in Manchester. **No, wait**, Liverpool.* |
| **Hang on** (*Espérate un segundo*) | *She has a Ford. **Hang on**, no, it's an Opel.* |
|  | *I have seven meetings this week. **Hang on**, eight.* |
| **Sorry, I mean…** (*quiero decir*) | *Summer is my favourite season. **Sorry, I mean** spring.* |
|  | *He sold his car three weeks ago. **Sorry, I mean** three years ago.* |

⚠️ **No, wait** (*no, espera*) ≠ **No way** (*ni de broma*).

💡 Keep the correction fast and simple — you can give just the right fact (*No, wait, six*) or a short sentence (*No, wait, it was six*).

sections.title: 3. Correcting Opinions
sections.content:
Correcting an opinion is more abstract, so we make the correction more **elaborate** — always say the full corrected sentence.

### Maybe *X* isn't the right word
- *Peter is a weird person. **Maybe weird isn't the right word.** He's peculiar.*
- *My boss is lazy. **Maybe lazy isn't the right word.** He's not very organised.*
- *The meeting was boring. **Maybe boring isn't the right word.** It was just too long.*
- *The new employee is arrogant. **Maybe arrogant isn't the right word.** He's too confident.*

### Let me put it another way (*dicho de otra forma*)
- *The hotel was dirty. **Let me put it another way.** It was messy.*
- *The contest was stupid. **Let me put it another way.** It was disappointing.*
- *He was a bad player. **Let me put it another way.** He wasn't in shape.*

sections.title: 4. When You Forget the Word
sections.content:
| Expression | Example |
|---|---|
| **What's the word?** / What's the word I'm looking for? | *I was looking for the… **what's the word?** Handle.* |
| **I can't think of the word.** | *The city was very… **I can't think of the word**… lively.* |
| **How can I put this?** (more natural than *How can I say this?*) | *The party was fun, but it was a little… **how can I put this?** Overwhelming.* |

📖 **handle** = *manillar* · **lively** = *animada* · **overwhelming** = *abrumadora*

qs.q: 'I saw my brother on Friday. ___, it was Thursday.'
What's the difference between 'No, wait' and 'No way'?
opts: 'No, wait' = no, espera; 'No way' = ni de broma
qs.ans: 'No, wait' = no, espera; 'No way' = ni de broma

qs.q: 'She has a Ford. ___, it's an Opel.'
Which phrase means 'quiero decir'?
'The meeting was boring. ___ It was just too long.'
opts: Maybe boring isn't the right word.
Maybe boring isn't the right way.
qs.ans: Maybe boring isn't the right word.

qs.q: How do you say 'dicho de otra forma'?
opts: Let me put it another way.
Let me tell it other way.
qs.ans: Let me put it another way.

qs.q: Which is the most natural way to say '¿cómo lo digo?'
What does 'overwhelming' mean?

title: Natural English
topic: Changing Meaning with Intonation

sections.title: 1. Intonation Changes Meaning
sections.content:
Intonation doesn't just make you sound natural — it can **change the meaning** of the exact same sentence. We do this in Spanish too (*Yo **no** dije que él robó el dinero*), so use the same instinct in English.

**How to stress a word:**
- Say it with **more intensity** and a change of **tone**.
- Add a short **pause** before or after it.

sections.title: 2. "I didn't say he stole the money."
sections.content:
| Stress | Implied meaning |
|---|---|
| *I **didn't** say he stole the money.* | It's simply **not true** — I never said it. |
| *I didn't **say** he stole the money.* | I didn't *say* it… but maybe I **implied** or wrote it. |
| *I didn't say **he** stole the money.* | Someone stole it — but it was **someone else**. |
| *I didn't say he **stole** the money.* | He did something else — maybe he **borrowed** it. |
| *I didn't say he stole the **money**.* | He stole **something else**. |

sections.title: 3. "She didn't ask how to do it."
sections.content:
| You want to say… | Stress |
|---|---|
| It wasn't her — it was another person. | ***She** didn't ask how to do it.* |
| It wasn't a question — she demanded it. | *She didn't **ask** how to do it.* |
| She asked how to do something else, not this. | *She didn't ask how to do **it**.* |
| It never happened. | *She **didn't** ask how to do it.* |
| She asked *why*, not *how*. | *She didn't ask **how** to do it.* |

sections.title: 4. "I really liked the film."
sections.content:
| You want to say… | Stress |
|---|---|
| The film was good, but everything else was a disaster. | *I really liked the **film**.* |
| **I** liked it — my friends, not so much. | ***I** really liked the film.* |
| Enthusiasm — it was amazing! | *I **really** liked the film.* |
| I liked it, but that's all — I didn't watch it to the end. | *I really **liked** the film.* |

💡 It feels like acting at first — that's normal. Play with stress when you talk to yourself and it will start to feel natural.

qs.q: You want to make clear it's completely false. Which word do you stress in 'I didn't say he stole the money'?
'I didn't SAY he stole the money.' What does it imply?
opts: I implied it, but didn't say it
qs.ans: I implied it, but didn't say it

qs.q: 'I didn't say HE stole the money.' What does it imply?
'I didn't say he STOLE the money.' What does it imply?
opts: He did something else with it, like borrowing it
qs.ans: He did something else with it, like borrowing it

qs.q: She asked WHY, not how. Which word do you stress in 'She didn't ask how to do it'?
You want to sound enthusiastic. Which word do you stress in 'I really liked the film'?
'I really liked the FILM.' What does it imply?
opts: The film was good, but other things weren't
qs.ans: The film was good, but other things weren't

qs.q: Besides a change of tone, what usually goes with the stressed word?
opts: A short pause before or after it
qs.ans: A short pause before or after it

title: Natural English
topic: Natural Idioms and How to Use Them

sections.title: 1. Learning Idioms the Right Way
sections.content:
Textbook idioms are often learned **in isolation** — so we never remember them in a real conversation — and many are **not the most natural** ones (some are rare or old-fashioned). Learn **a few**, practise them **in context** and **orally**, then add more.

🇬🇧 Several of these are especially **British**; *fingers crossed*, *touch wood* and *not my cup of tea* are understood everywhere.

sections.title: 2. Gutted & Chuffed
sections.content:
| Adjective | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **gutted** | very disappointed / sad (from *gut* = *tripas*) | *I'm **gutted** she didn't tell me the truth.* |
| **chuffed** | very pleased / proud | *I'm **chuffed** with my new boss.* |

Exaggerate even more with **absolutely**: *I'm **absolutely gutted** / **absolutely chuffed**.*

⚠️ They describe **your feelings**, not your opinion of a thing — a dress can be *right up your street*, but it can't make you *chuffed* by itself.

sections.title: 3. Fingers Crossed & Touch Wood
sections.content:
| Español | English | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Crucemos los dedos | **Fingers crossed** (not *let's cross our fingers*) | ***Fingers crossed** I win the prize.* |
| Toquemos madera | **Touch wood** (no *let's*) | *We're healthy now, **touch wood**.* |

💡 Fixed expressions keep their order: *fingers crossed* — the adjective goes **after** the noun. And you don't need *I have my fingers crossed* — just ***fingers crossed***.

sections.title: 4. Right Up My Street & Not My Cup of Tea
sections.content:
| Expression | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **It's right up my street** (🇺🇸 *right up my alley*) | I really like it — it's exactly my kind of thing | *A painting of a lake? **It's right up my street.*** |
| **It's not my cup of tea** | I don't like it (a classic!) | *The opera? Sorry, **it's not my cup of tea**.* |

sections.title: 5. Practice
sections.content:
### Rephrase with an idiom

| Standard | With the idiom |
|---|---|
| I want to be sure we don't have any problems. | **Touch wood** we don't have any problems. |
| I don't want to go to the beach. I don't really like it. | I don't want to go to the beach. **It's not my cup of tea.** |
| Let's hope they don't fire him. | **Fingers crossed** they don't fire him. |
| I'm so disappointed she didn't tell me the truth. | I'm so **gutted** she didn't tell me the truth. |
| I'd love to go to a Chinese restaurant. I really like it. | I'd love to go to a Chinese restaurant. **It's right up my street.** |
| I'm so pleased we're finally getting married. | I'm so **chuffed** we're finally getting married. |

### Translate

| Español | English |
|---|---|
| Crucemos los dedos de que el niño no esté perdido. | **Fingers crossed** the child isn't lost. |
| Gracias por el vestido, es mi rollo total. | Thank you for the dress, **it's right up my street**. |
| Estoy encantada con mi nuevo jefe. | I'm **chuffed** with my new boss. |
| Tenemos todo lo necesario, toquemos madera. | We have everything we need, **touch wood**. |
| Estoy decepcionadísima con el resultado. | I'm **gutted** with the result. |

qs.q: You lost something with a lot of sentimental value. How do you feel?
You finally got the job you wanted for years. How do you feel?
How do you say 'Crucemos los dedos'?
How do you say 'Toquemos madera'?
A friend invites you to the opera, but you hate opera. What do you say?
opts: It's not my cup of tea.
qs.ans: It's not my cup of tea.

qs.q: Someone shows you a painting of a lake, and you love lakes:
'Thank you for the dress, ___'
Which is the American version of 'right up my street'?

title: Natural English
topic: Asking Questions Naturally

sections.title: 1. Alternatives to *Why*
sections.content:
*Why* is fine, but using it all the time sounds like an interrogation. Two natural alternatives:

### What made you + verb? (*¿Qué te hizo…?*) — for past decisions

| With why | Natural |
|---|---|
| Why did you do that? | **What made you do** that? |
| Why did you move to London? | **What made you move** to London? |
| Why did you choose that university? | **What made you choose** that university? |
| Why did you change your mind? | **What made you change** your mind? |

⚠️ *made* is past, and the next verb is the **bare** form — not ~~*to change*~~.

### How come…? (*¿Cómo es que…?*) — any tense, softer and more conversational

**No auxiliary, no inversion** — just the sentence:

| With why | Natural |
|---|---|
| Why did you move to London? | **How come** you moved to London? |
| Why did you leave so early? | **How come** you left so early? |
| Why didn't you eat meat? | **How come** you didn't eat meat? |
| Why are you coming? | **How come** you're coming? |
| Why will you sell the house? | **How come** you'll sell the house? |
| Why does she practise padel? | **How come** she practises padel? |

sections.title: 2. Short Follow-Up Questions
sections.content:
Start with a full question, then keep the conversation rolling with **short** ones — like in Spanish. They're not bad grammar; they only work in conversation.

| Full question | Short version |
|---|---|
| What did you think about the ending? | **And the ending?** |
| Who did you go with? | **Who with?** (you'll also hear *With who?*) |
| When did you go? | **When?** |
| How much did it cost? | **How much?** |
| What happened afterwards? | **And then what?** |

sections.title: 3. Whereabouts?
sections.content:
To ask for the **exact location** (*¿dónde exactamente?*) use **whereabouts** — one word, with an *s*. Very common in British English.

- *I'm from Italy.* — *Oh, amazing. **Whereabouts?***
- *I'm going to Portugal next month.* — ***Whereabouts in Portugal?***
- *The party is in an amazing place.* — ***Whereabouts is the party?***

sections.title: 4. Conversation, Not Interview
sections.content:
Firing basic questions one after another (*Where do you live? Are you married? Do you have children?*) sounds like an **interview**. React and connect instead:

> **A:** I'm from Scotland.
> **B:** Oh, really? **Whereabouts** in Scotland?
> **A:** Edinburgh.
> **B:** That's nice. So when did you move?
> **A:** Five years ago.
> **B:** Interesting — **what made you move?** / **How come you moved?**

### Practice
- *I started a new job last month.* — *Oh, that's great. **How's it going?***
- *I needed to leave my company.* — ***How come** you left your company?*
- *I've decided to move abroad.* — ***Whereabouts?*** … ***What made you** want to move abroad?*
- *We're going to the party tonight.* — ***Who with?*** … ***How come** you decided to go?*

qs.q: 'Why did you move to London?' → with 'make':
opts: What made you move to London?
What made you to move to London?
What did make you move to London?
What makes you moved to London?
qs.ans: What made you move to London?

qs.q: 'Why did you leave so early?' → with 'how come':
opts: How come did you leave so early?
How come you left so early?
How come you did leave so early?
qs.ans: How come you left so early?

qs.q: 'Why does she practise padel?' → with 'how come':
opts: How come does she practise padel?

qs.q: Which alternative to 'why' works in ANY tense?
'I went to a concert last night.' You want to know their companion:
'I'm going to Portugal next month.' You want the exact place:
'I bought a jacket yesterday.' You want to know the price:
Why use short follow-up questions?
opts: They keep the conversation natural, not like an interview
qs.ans: They keep the conversation natural, not like an interview

title: Natural English
topic: Combining Adverbs + Adjectives

sections.title: 1. Beyond *Very* and *Really*
sections.content: *Very*, *really* and *extremely* work with almost everything, so learners overuse them. Natives choose the adverb that **matches the adjective** — technically correct isn't always natural.

sections.title: 2. Extreme Adjectives → *Absolutely*
sections.content:
Some adjectives are already the **exaggerated** version. Don't use *very* with them — the adverb has to match the intensity: use **absolutely** (or **completely**).

| Neutral | Extreme | Natural combo |
|---|---|---|
| cold | **freezing** | It's **absolutely freezing**. |
| tired | **exhausted** | I'm **absolutely exhausted**. |
| scared | **terrified** | I'm **absolutely terrified**. |
| glad / happy | **delighted** | I'm **absolutely delighted**. |
| silly | **ridiculous** | This is **absolutely ridiculous**. |

🗣️ Stress the **A**: ***AB**-so-lute-ly*.

⚠️ **terrific** sounds scary but means **great**: *The movie was terrific!*

sections.title: 3. Emotional Adjectives → *Deeply*
sections.content:
Emotions are felt *inside*, so the natural intensifier is **deeply**, for positive and negative feelings alike.

- I'm **deeply disappointed**.
- I'm **deeply offended**.
- I'm **deeply grateful**.
- I'm **deeply concerned**.
- I'm **deeply unhappy**.

💡 *Bitterly* and *painfully* also exist, but they're more specific (negative only). *Deeply* is the universal one.

sections.title: 4. Judgements & Recommendations → *Highly*
sections.content:
When there's a **subjective judgement**, qualification or recommendation, use **highly**.

- It's **highly recommended**.
- It's **highly successful**.
- It's **highly controversial**.
- It's **highly unlikely**.
- It's **highly effective**.
- It's **highly competitive**.

qs.q: What's the extreme version of 'cold'?
Most natural: 'It's ___ freezing.'
Most natural: 'I'm ___ delighted.'
What's the extreme version of 'silly'?
Most natural: 'I'm ___ disappointed.'
Most natural: 'I'm ___ grateful.'
Most natural: 'It's ___ recommended.'
Most natural: 'It's ___ unlikely.'
'The movie was terrific!' What does it mean?

title: Natural English
topic: Modifying Meaning with Adverbs

sections.title: 1. One Adjective, Different Messages
sections.content: Continuing from Sep 18: with the **same adjective**, changing the adverb changes the **intention** of the message — a creative alternative to always using *very* and *really*.

sections.title: 2. Surprised
sections.content:
🗣️ **surprised** — the first syllable almost disappears; the stress is on ***-prised***.

| Adverb | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **genuinely** | the surprise is real, authentic (*truly* also works) | *I was **genuinely surprised** when she called.* |
| **pleasantly** | a positive surprise | *I was **pleasantly surprised** by the hotel.* |
| **slightly** | only a little — you half expected it | *I was **slightly surprised** because he didn't come.* |
| **completely** | no expectations at all | *We were **completely surprised** by the announcement.* |

🗣️ **genuinely** — the *n* sounds almost like a Spanish *ñ*: *GEN-yu-in-ly* · **pleasantly** — *PLEZ-ant-ly*, not *please*.

⚠️ **hardly** = *apenas* (barely), **not** *a little*: *I was hardly surprised* = I was barely surprised.

sections.title: 3. Concerned
sections.content:
**Concerned** = worried (*preocupado*) — it already has a slightly negative touch.

| Adverb | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **slightly** | a small concern | *I'm **slightly concerned**.* |
| **genuinely** | an honest, authentic concern | *I'm **genuinely concerned**.* |
| **deeply** | a strong emotional concern (emotions → *deeply*) | *I'm **deeply concerned**.* |
| **seriously** | it's not a joke — important, even grave | *I'm **seriously concerned**.* |

sections.title: 4. Practice — Pick the Combo
sections.content:
| Context | Combo |
|---|---|
| You expected the restaurant to be terrible, but it was good. | **pleasantly surprised** |
| You weren't pretending — you really didn't expect it. | **genuinely surprised** |
| You had absolutely no idea. | **completely surprised** |
| You expected it a little, but it still surprised you. | **slightly surprised** |

qs.q: You weren't pretending — the surprise was real:
You expected the restaurant to be terrible, but it was good:
You half expected it, but it still surprised you a little:
You had absolutely no idea:
What does 'I was hardly surprised' mean?
opts: I was surprised in a hard way

qs.q: Your concern is strong and emotional:
Your concern is not a joke — it's important:
What does 'concerned' mean?

title: Natural English
topic: Quite and Not Quite / I Wouldn't Say…

sections.title: 1. Quite (*bastante*)
sections.content:
**Quite** (also *pretty*, *fairly*) works with the adjective — its meaning depends on how **intense** the adjective is:

| Adjective type | Meaning of *quite* | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Neutral / mild** (good, bad, tricky) | **A** — a decent amount, enough but not excessive (could also take *very*) | *The film was **quite good**.* · *The exam was **quite tricky**.* · *The show was **quite bad**.* |
| **Extreme / absolute** (impossible, sure, exhausted) | **B** — completely, totally (*very* would sound wrong) | *That's **quite impossible**.* · *I'm **quite sure** that's what happened.* · *I'm **quite exhausted**.* |

💡 Some adjectives depend on context — *She's **quite upset*** can be mild or strong. It's a question of nuance, not a grammar mistake.

sections.title: 2. Not Quite (*no del todo*)
sections.content:
A very natural answer when something is **almost, but not exactly** true — then add a clarification. Softer than a direct *no*.

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| So are you angry with him? | **Not quite.** I'm disappointed. |
| Is it finished? | **Not quite.** I have a couple more things to do. |
| So it's basically the same thing? | **Not quite.** There are a few differences. |
| Are you ready? | **Not quite.** I have to do a couple of things. |
| So you don't like your job? | **Not quite.** I like it, but I find it stressful. |
| So you're saying we shouldn't go? | **Not quite.** I think we should go, but a little later. |
| So the problem is the price? | **Not quite.** I don't like the quality. |
| So you felt sad at the wedding? | **Not quite.** I felt more nostalgic than sad. |

💡 *Not exactly* is similar, but *not quite* often fits better (*Are you ready? — Not quite.*). *Not yet* only works for actions that haven't happened — *So you're angry? — Not yet* means you **will** be!

sections.title: 3. I Wouldn't Say…, I'd Say…
sections.content:
Deny gently with the **conditional** — *Yo no diría que…, diría que…* — instead of a blunt *No, I don't*.

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| So you hate your job? | **I wouldn't say** I hate my job, **I'd say** I'm bored of it. |
| So you're very sociable? | **I wouldn't say** I'm sociable, **I'd say** I have a lot of social skills. |
| So you're a very organised person? | **I wouldn't say** I'm an organised person, **I'd say** I'm good at planning things. |
| So you don't like cooking? | **I wouldn't say** I don't like cooking, **I'd say** I don't cook very often. |

### With *just* (*simplemente*)

| Español | English |
|---|---|
| No diría que no me gustan los gatos, diría que prefiero los perros. | I wouldn't say I don't like cats, **I'd say** I prefer dogs. |
| No diría que no me gusta el dulce, simplemente prefiero lo salado. | I wouldn't say I don't like sweet things, **I just** prefer **savoury** things. |

📖 *salado* (food) = **savoury**, not *salty*.

tests.title: Test · Quite, Not Quite & I Wouldn't Say

qs.q: 'The film was quite good.' What does 'quite' mean here?
'That's quite impossible.' What does 'quite' mean here?
Which synonym can replace 'quite' in 'quite good'?
'Is it finished?' — It's almost done:
opts: Not quite. I have a couple more things to do.
Quite not. I have a couple more things to do.
qs.ans: Not quite. I have a couple more things to do.

qs.q: 'So you felt sad at the wedding?' — You felt nostalgic:
opts: Not quite. I felt more nostalgic than sad.
No, I wasn't sad at all.
qs.ans: Not quite. I felt more nostalgic than sad.

qs.q: 'So you hate your job?' — You're just bored of it:
opts: I wouldn't say I hate my job, I'd say I'm bored of it.
I won't say I hate my job, I say I'm bored of it.
I wouldn't said I hate my job.
I don't would say I hate my job.
qs.ans: I wouldn't say I hate my job, I'd say I'm bored of it.

qs.q: 'Simplemente prefiero lo salado.'
Why answer with 'I wouldn't say…' instead of 'No'?
opts: It sounds gentler and more natural
qs.ans: It sounds gentler and more natural

title: English Time with Juls
topic: Adjectives to Describe Food / Make vs Do

sections.title: 1. Adjectives to Describe Food & Drinks
sections.content:
A set of adjectives to describe food and drinks, practised as an *Ask me* exercise (you ask the question, then answer it).

| Adjective | Spanish | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **drinkable** | potable | *drink* → *drinkable* — simple logic |
| **edible** | comestible | ⚠ Not *eatable* — the logical form doesn't exist; we say **edible** |
| **tasty** | sabroso, rico | Very common, used a lot in restaurants |
| **mouthwatering** | que se te hace la boca agua | One word, no hyphen — another way to say *very tasty* |
| **delicious** | delicioso | Pronounce /dɪˈlɪʃəs/ — closed *de-*, not a Spanish *deli-* |
| **savory** (US) / **savoury** (UK) | salado (as a category) | The opposite of *sweet* |
| **tender** | tierno, blandito | Meat, vegetables… |

### Savory vs. salty
- **savory** = salty food as a **general category** — the opposite of sweet: *Do you prefer sweet or savory food?*
- **salty** = something that really has **added salt** (salted nuts, popcorn…)

### Pronunciation: -ous endings
Words ending in **-ous** are pronounced with a weak /əs/: *delicious* /dɪˈlɪʃəs/. Pay attention to the start of the word too: closed **de-**, not an open Spanish *deli-*.

### Practice (Ask me…)
- Is the water drinkable? → Yes, the water is drinkable.
- Are you sure that product was edible? → No, I'm not sure that product was edible.
- Did you bring something tasty for a snack? → Yes, I brought something tasty for a snack.
- Was everything at the table mouthwatering? → Yes, everything at the table was mouthwatering.
- Was the food at the wedding delicious? → Yes, the food at the wedding was delicious.
- Do you prefer sweet or savory food?
- Was your lunch tender? → Yes, my lunch was tender.

sections.title: 2. Make vs. Do
sections.content:
Don't memorise long lists — learn a few rules and incorporate examples little by little.

### DO — activities in general
Anything you put into practice, any general action:
- **do** homework, exercise, a course, business, well, a favor

### MAKE — three useful rules

| Rule | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Create / build** something | make a cake, make coffee, make dinner, make friends *(you create a friendship)*, make a reservation |
| **Plans** | make a plan, make a choice, make an arrangement |
| **Anything that involves speaking** | make a speech, make a complaint, make a wish, make a comment, make a confession, make a promise |

> **Tip:** think of *create*, not just *build* — you don't build friends or a reservation, but you **create** them.

Combinations that don't fit any rule: just remember the collocation and repeat it many times.

### Practice
- Harry **is doing** an online course at the moment.
- Bob **did** a favor for me last night. *(a general action)*
- My boss **will make** a speech tomorrow. *(speaking)*
- My sister **makes** a wish every birthday. *(speaking, even if it's said quietly)*
- The employees **did** business at the conference last week. *(a general action: you negotiate, take notes, write reports…)*

### Pronunciation note: *often*
Both /ˈɒfən/ (silent T) and /ˈɒftən/ are correct — it depends on the accent.

qs.q: What does 'edible' mean?
Which word is correct?
'The water is drinkable' means the water is…
What does 'mouthwatering' mean?
opts: So tasty it makes your mouth water
qs.ans: So tasty it makes your mouth water

qs.q: Which word describes salty food as a general category (the opposite of sweet)?
'My lunch was tender' means the food was…

Harry ___ an online course at the moment.

title: English Time with Juls
topic: To Give Up On / Silent B

sections.title: 1. Discussion: Bungee Jumping & Taking Risks
sections.content:
Juls tells the story of her first bungee jump (from a bridge near Buitrago de Lozoya) and how it compares with skydiving.

### Useful vocabulary from the conversation

| Word / expression | Spanish |
|---|---|
| **a bruise** | un moratón |
| **a harness** | un arnés |
| **to be attached (at the waist)** | estar sujeto/a (por la cintura) |
| **to hang** / **hanging** | colgar / colgando |
| **fearful** | miedoso/a |
| **clumsy** | torpe |
| **overprotective** | sobreprotector/a |
| **reckless** | imprudente, temerario/a |
| **thoroughly** | a fondo, minuciosamente |
| **to ramble** | enrollarse, divagar |
| **the anticipation is always worse** | la espera siempre es peor |

### Expressions
- *I have never driven **whilst** being drunk.*
- *The older we get, the more fearful we become.* — the **the + comparative, the + comparative** structure.
- *Your fears become a condition for your children.*

sections.title: 2. Phrasal Verb: To Give Up On
sections.content:
**To give up on someone / something** = to **lose hope** in someone or something — *perder la esperanza en, rendirse (emocionalmente) con*.

| Verb | Type | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **give up** | Intransitive — no object | *I give up.* (Me rindo.) |
| **give up on** + object | Transitive — needs an object | *I gave up on politicians.* / *Don't give up on me.* |

> It's very emotional: use it for a person who disappoints you, a dream that isn't coming true, a goal you no longer have… Some phrasal verbs have **two particles** (*give* + *up* + *on*), and you need both.

⚠ Not *give up with*, *give in* or *despair* (*despair* = desesperación, a noun).

### Practice
- She **gave up on** the project yesterday. → Why did she give up on the project yesterday?
- The boss **will give up on** the team soon. → Why will the boss give up on the team soon?
- I **am about to give up on** you. → Why am I about to give up on you? *(about to = estar a punto de)*
- They **have already given up on** Susan. → Why have they already given up on Susan?
- The technician **is giving up on** the problem as we speak. → Why is the technician giving up on the problem as we speak?
- She **never gives up on** her friends. → Why **doesn't** she **ever** give up on her friends?
- The candidate **gave up on** the interview this morning. → Why did the candidate give up on the interview this morning?

### *Never* in questions → negative auxiliary + *ever*
English avoids double negatives, so in a question *never* becomes **negative auxiliary + ever**:
- *¿Por qué nunca vienes conmigo?* → **Why don't you ever** come with me?
- **Why doesn't she ever** tell me the truth?

sections.title: 3. Silent B Pronunciation
sections.content:
In many words ending in **-mb** (and a few others) the **B is silent**. It's easier to learn the word by ear before you see the spelling.

| Word | Pronunciation | Spanish |
|---|---|---|
| **plumber** | /ˈplʌmə/ | fontanero |
| **climbing** | /ˈklaɪmɪŋ/ | escalar, escalada |
| **numb** | /nʌm/ | adormecido, entumecido |
| **bomb** | /bɒm/ | bomba |
| **lamb** | /læm/ | cordero |

*Numb* is already an adjective, so no *-ed*: *My hands get numb.* (Remember Linkin Park's *Numb*: "I've become so numb…")

### Practice (Ask me…)
- How much does a plumber cost?
- Do you fancy going climbing this weekend?
- Do your hands get numb when you are cold?
- What would you do if you found a bomb?
- Did you have a baby lamb in your garden?

opts: To stop talking to someone for a day

qs.q: What is the difference between 'give up' and 'give up on'?
opts: 'Give up' has no object; 'give up on' needs an object
'Give up on' is only for the past
qs.ans: 'Give up' has no object; 'give up on' needs an object

qs.q: They / Susan / already →
opts: They have already given up on Susan.
They already gave up with Susan.
They have already give up on Susan.
qs.ans: They have already given up on Susan.

qs.q: I / about to / you →
opts: I am about to give up on you.
I am about giving up you.
I about to give up on you.
qs.ans: I am about to give up on you.

qs.q: The technician / the problem / as we speak →
opts: The technician gives up on the problem as we speak.
The technician is giving up on the problem as we speak.
The technician gave up the problem as we speak.
qs.ans: The technician is giving up on the problem as we speak.

qs.q: 'She never gives up on her friends.' Ask why:
opts: Why does she never gives up on her friends?
Why doesn't she ever give up on her friends?
Why doesn't she never give up on her friends?
qs.ans: Why doesn't she ever give up on her friends?

title: English Time with Juls
topic: To Give Off / Next Few & Last Few

sections.title: 1. Phrasal Verb: To Give Off
sections.content:
**To give off** = *emitir, desprender, dar, liberar*. It has two uses:

| Use | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Literal** | Emit something physical: heat, a smell, a gas, radiation | *A light bulb gives off heat.* |
| **Figurative** | Transmit a feeling or energy you can't measure | *My boss gives off an air of superiority.* |

### Don't confuse with other *give* phrasal verbs
- **give out** = *repartir, distribuir* (intentional)
- **give in** = *ceder, sucumbir*
- **give off** = something more automatic, not necessarily done on purpose

> **Phrasal verb vs. Latin synonym:** *emit* exists, but like most Latin-based verbs it sounds formal and is mostly used in writing. In everyday speech, prefer **give off**.

### Practice (Ask me…)
- Does a **light bulb** *(bombilla)* give off heat? → Yes, a light bulb gives off heat.
- Do flowers give off a **fragrant** smell? → Yes, flowers give off a fragrant smell.
- Do you think pregnant women give off a **glow** *(un brillo, un resplandor)*? → Yes, I think pregnant women give off a glow.
- Does your boss give off an air of superiority? → No, my boss doesn't give off an air of superiority.
- Does a black hole give off radiation? → Yes, a black hole gives off radiation.
- Do you dress to give off a good impression?

### Translations
- *Las flores son bonitas, pero desprenden un mal olor.* → The flowers are beautiful, but they **give off** a bad smell.
- *No sé lo que es, pero (ella) desprende una mala vibración.* → I don't know what it is, but she **gives off** a bad vibration / a bad **vibe**.
- *No puedo estar cerca de ti, desprendes mucho calor.* → I can't be close to you, you **give off** too much heat.

sections.title: 2. The Next Few / The Last Few
sections.content:
In Spanish we say *en los próximos días* / *en los últimos días*. In English *the next days* / *the last days* is not quite right: you need **few**.

| ❌ | ✅ |
|---|---|
| in the next days | **for the next few days** |
| in the last weeks | **for the last few weeks** |

> When you express the **duration** of an action, use the preposition **for**: *for the next few days* (= durante los próximos días).

### Practice
- I'll be in Milan **for the next few days**. → Why will you be in Milan for the next few days?
- He has been working with John **for the last few weeks**.
- They will have / will be having a meeting **for the next few hours**. → Why will they be having a meeting for the next few hours?
- We will practice this **for the next few minutes**. → Why will we practice this for the next few minutes?
- It has been very difficult **for the last few months**. → Why has it been very difficult for the last few months?

With *the last few…* use the **present perfect** when the period hasn't finished. With *the next few…* use the future simple or the future continuous (more sense of continuity).

title: English Time with Juls
topic: Motivation for New Students

sections.title: 1. How Juls Learned English
sections.content:
A special class: instead of a grammar point, Juls answers a student's question, *"Would you mind explaining your process of learning English?"*

### No special situation
People assume she has English family, lived abroad or studied in England. **None of that is true**: 100% Spanish family, always lived in her hometown, never been to England (only a weekend in Ireland).

### What she did (from about age 12)
- School + a traditional English academy: useful, but **not the secret**.
- **The secret:** surrounding herself with English in her free time, mainly **YouTube**, always choosing the English version, with no subtitles or dubbing back then.
- At first she understood only ~40% (despite good marks at school). Instead of **giving up**, she kept listening, and understood more and more each time. We repeat the same words, expressions and structures all the time, so the brain builds **associations**.
- **Shadowing** (imitation): repeating out loud what she heard, e.g. *"Oh, I'm so excited!"* (*¡Qué ilusión!*), speaking to herself, for fun.

> It doesn't happen **overnight**: the brain needs time to build **solid** associations and make the language **automatic**, **second nature**. Progress isn't even, but it *is* progress, and seeing it keeps you motivated.

sections.title: 2. Practical Tips
sections.content:
### What to listen to
- Content with **one, two or three people max**: monologues, interviews, one- or two-person podcasts, someone speaking to the camera, radio shows.
- Avoid starting with **films**: strong accents, complex plots, lots of names… they can **destroy your motivation**.
- Find speakers who **enunciate**, have a clear accent, pause and don't speak too fast (*speaking fast is overrated*). When you find someone you understand, **stay with them**, then move on progressively.

### English is a tool, not the goal
English is the **door** to content, people and knowledge. Don't obsess over every word; focus on understanding *what the person is saying* about a topic you love.
- Example from a student: learning to draw with a drawing book **in English**.

### The only homework: speak
Take what you practised in class and **use it out loud** all day, talking about real things:
> *The other day I **bought** some bananas, and they weren't very good. Then I **bought** some apples, and those were better…*

Don't fill pages of written exercises: speaking is what's most effective.

### Juls's one-line summary
**Have fun when you learn English. Use it as a tool, not the objective. Learn about things you enjoy, in English. Speak to yourself.**

sections.title: 3. Learning Philosophy & Vocabulary
sections.content:
- **If it's not enjoyable, it's not effective.** Children love learning until school makes it strict and serious. When you enjoy the process, your brain is *high on dopamine* and absorbs much more.
- The rigid system of classes by age and exams to move on grew out of the **Industrial Revolution**, which needed efficient workers. Juls wishes for a balance between training and the joy of learning.
- A teacher should be a **guide** and a **catalyst** (*catalizador*), not a source of dogma.
- Be **gentle and compassionate** with yourself, and **don't be too hard on yourself**.

### Useful vocabulary

| Expression | Spanish |
|---|---|
| **second nature** | algo que te sale de forma natural/automática |
| **it doesn't happen overnight** | no ocurre de la noche a la mañana |
| **shadowing** | imitar en voz alta lo que escuchas |
| **to enunciate** | articular/vocalizar bien |
| **overwhelming** | abrumador |
| **a chore** | una tarea pesada, una obligación |
| **to ramble** | enrollarse, divagar |
| **to be keen on (doing) something** | tener muchas ganas de / gustarle mucho algo |
| **don't be too hard on yourself** | no seas tan duro/a contigo mismo/a |
| **a catalyst** | un catalizador |

opts: Living in England as a teenager
Surrounding herself with English in her free time (YouTube) and repeating out loud
qs.ans: Surrounding herself with English in her free time (YouTube) and repeating out loud

qs.q: What is 'shadowing'?
opts: Imitating and repeating out loud what you hear
qs.ans: Imitating and repeating out loud what you hear

qs.q: What kind of content does Juls recommend to start with?
opts: Content with one to three people: interviews, monologues, podcasts
qs.ans: Content with one to three people: interviews, monologues, podcasts

opts: It takes time; it isn't immediate
qs.ans: It takes time; it isn't immediate

opts: A tool, a door to content you enjoy

qs.ans: A tool, a door to content you enjoy

qs.ans: I'm very interested in learning to draw

title: English Time with Juls
topic: I Wish

sections.title: 1. Discussion: World Cup Champions
sections.content:
The day after Spain won the World Cup final against Argentina, Juls talks about the match, the nerves, and her one swimming competition as a child.

### Useful vocabulary

| Word / expression | Spanish |
|---|---|
| **a snippet** | un trocito, un fragmento (of a video, film or match) |
| **an own goal** | un gol en propia puerta |
| **to be biased** | estar sesgado/a |
| **the cherry on top** | la guinda del pastel (often ironic) |
| **to shake like a leaf** | temblar como una hoja |
| **it's not worth it** | no merece la pena |
| **class and elegance** | clase y elegancia |
| **despicable** | despreciable |
| **a ginger / a redhead** | un pelirrojo / una pelirroja |
| **a crush** | un enamoramiento, un amor platónico |

### *Like* vs. *fancy*
- **I like someone** = *me cae bien*.
- **I fancy someone** = *me gusta* (I find them attractive). *The one that I fancied in 2010 was Xabi Alonso.*

### Summer schedule (July 2026)
Monday and Wednesday classes move to **4:30** for the rest of July; Friday stays at 2:00 PM. Plus a **summer intensive week** at the start of August.

sections.title: 2. I Wish (Ojalá)
sections.content:
**Ojalá** (a word from Arabic) has no direct translation, but its English equivalent is **I wish** (you wish, he wishes…).

English has no subjunctive (*tuviera/tuviese*), so it uses the **past simple** to talk about a **hypothetical** present:

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Ojalá **tuviera** más dinero. | I wish I **had** more money. |
| Ojalá **fuera** rico. | I wish I **were** rich. |
| Ojalá **pudiera** venir. | I wish they **could** come. |

### *Were* for every subject
In hypothetical sentences, *to be* is **were** for all subjects: *I wish I **were** rich.* Many natives say *was*, and it may end up accepted, but the rule is **were**.

### ⚠ Not *would*
*Would* is the conditional (*ojalá se comportarían* ❌). Use the past simple:
- ❌ *I wish her children would be better behaved.*
- ✅ *I wish her children **weren't** so badly behaved.*

### Wishes about the past → past perfect
If the situation is already in the past, go one step back: **past perfect**.
- *It's too bad she couldn't attend the conference.* → I wish she **had been able to** attend the conference. / I wish she **could have attended** the conference.
- *Can* has no participle, so use **be able to**.

### Practice (It's a pity… → I wish…)
- It's a pity he doesn't speak English. → I wish he **spoke** / **could speak** English.
- It's a pity they can't come to the party. → I wish they **could** come to the party.
- It's a shame I'm not rich. → I wish I **were** rich.
- It's a pity her children are so badly behaved. → I wish her children **weren't** so badly behaved.
- It's too bad she couldn't attend the conference. → I wish she **had been able to** attend the conference.
- It's a pity he loses his wallet so often. → I wish he **didn't lose** his wallet so often.
- It's a pity that she doesn't have a nice boyfriend. → I wish she **had** a nice boyfriend.

title: English Time with Juls
topic: To Run Out Of

sections.title: 1. Discussion: The News & Taking a Break
sections.content:
After a weekend of wildfires in Spain, Juls explains why she hardly ever watches the news, and why a summer break from English is fine.

### Useful vocabulary

| Expression | Spanish |
|---|---|
| **How are you doing?** | ¿Qué tal estás? *(= How are you? — not "what are you doing?")* |
| **ashes** | cenizas |
| **air quality** | calidad del aire |
| **I'd rather be uninformed than…** | prefiero estar desinformada que… |
| **polarized** | polarizado/a |
| **enough is enough** | ya basta |
| **to cross the line** | pasarse de la raya |
| **a blank canvas** / **a clean slate** | un lienzo en blanco / borrón y cuenta nueva *(⚠ not "white canvas")* |
| **engraved in your subconscious** | grabado en tu subconsciente |
| **to resume (a routine)** | retomar (una rutina) |

> **Taking a break won't make you forget your English.** When you come back, you often discover how much has become automatic, and that's great motivation.

sections.title: 2. To Run Out Of
sections.content:
**To run out of something** = *quedarse sin algo*. You need **both** particles: **out** + **of**.

*To be left without* isn't wrong, but **run out of** is much more natural.

### Pronunciation: make it one "pack"
Connect the words so they sound like one long word: **run-out-of** → /rʌnaʊtəv/. It's about **connection**, not speed. You can say it slowly with no gaps.
- Present **run** /rʌn/ vs. past **ran** /ræn/: *We **ran** out of petrol last week.*
- Third person: *My boss usually **runs out of** ideas.* The S links nicely to the vowel in *out*.

### Where to pause
- Before **extra information** (time, place): *We ran out of petrol | last week.*
- Between **two clauses**: *I run out of patience | when I can't understand something.*

### Practice (answer in the positive)
- Have you run out of milk today? → Yes, I've run out of milk today.
- Are we running out of time? → Yes, we are running out of time.
- Did you run out of petrol last week? → Yes, we ran out of petrol last week.
- Do you run out of patience when you can't understand something? → Yes, I run out of patience when I can't understand something.
- Will you run out of **breath** if you jump up and down? → Yes, I will run out of breath if I jump up and down.
- Does your boss usually run out of ideas? → Yes, my boss usually runs out of ideas.
- Has your car ever run out of battery? → Yes, my car has run out of battery **before**.
- Will you run out of energy if you go to bed at 2:00 a.m.? → Yes, I will run out of energy if I go to bed at 2:00 a.m.

### Translations
- *Él no se lava el pelo cuando se queda sin champú.* → He doesn't wash **his** hair when he runs out of shampoo.
- *No puedo ofrecerte desayuno porque nos hemos quedado sin pan.* → I can't offer you breakfast because we ran out of bread.
- *No puedo imprimir el documento. ¿Nos hemos quedado sin tinta?* → I can't print the document. Have we run out of ink?
- *Los niños siempre se quedan sin excusas.* → (The) children always run out of excuses.
- *Nos quedaremos sin gasolina si no vamos a una gasolinera pronto.* → We'll run out of petrol if we don't go to a petrol station soon.

sections.title: 3. Grammar Notes from the Practice
sections.content:
### Answering *Have you ever…?*
- Negative: **never** → *My car has **never** run out of battery.*
- Positive: ⚠ not *ever*. Answer plainly, or add **before** at the end (= *alguna vez*): *My car has run out of battery **before**.* / *Yes, I've been to China before.*
- The present perfect can't take an exact time. With an exact time, use the past simple: *My car ran out of battery **last week**.*

### Match the tense of the question
Asked in the present perfect → answer in the present perfect. Asked with *will* → answer with *will*. Other tenses aren't horrible, but they break the connection between question and answer.

### breathe vs. breath
- **breathe** /briːð/ = verb (*respirar*)
- **breath** /breθ/ = noun (*respiración, aliento*) → *run out of breath*

### Possessives with body parts
English always uses a possessive: *He washes **his** hair* (not *the hair*).

### Kids vs. children
Synonyms. **Kids** is a bit more American and colloquial. Both mean *niños* **and** *hijos*: *My kids are 50.*

### Children vs. the children
- *Children always run out of excuses* = children in general.
- *The children…* = a specific group.

title: English Time with Juls
topic: If Only / 3 Acronyms

sections.title: 1. If Only
sections.content:
First class of the **summer intensive week** (Mon–Thu 4:30, Fri 2:00 PM).

**If only…** = *si tan solo…, ojalá…*, a variation of **I wish** (see Jul 20).

| | Structure | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Hypothetical **present** | if only + subject + **past simple** | *If only I **had** more money.* |
| Hypothetical **past** | if only + subject + **past perfect** (*had* + participle) | *If only I **had known** the truth.* |

⚠ The word order is **if only I…**, not *if I only…* or *I only…*

### *If only* vs. *I wish*
*I wish* needs two subjects and sounds personal (*I wish Pepito had a bigger house*). *If only* needs just **one subject**, so it's a more general wish: *If only he had a bigger house.*

### Don't include *want*
You're not wishing to *want* something; you want the action itself to happen:
- ❌ *If only I wanted to stop saying…*
- ✅ *If only I **stopped** saying inappropriate things in front of my parents-in-law.*

### Practice: present
- He wants to speak English. → If only he **spoke** / **could speak** English.
- They want to be able to come to the wedding. → If only they **were able to** come to the wedding.
- You want to stop saying inappropriate things in front of your parents-in-law. → If only I **didn't say** / **stopped saying** inappropriate things in front of my parents-in-law.
- You want to know what your boss knows. → If only I **knew** what my boss knows.
- Your mother doesn't want to run out of coffee every week. → If only my mother **didn't run out** of coffee every week.

### Practice: past
- You wanted to say the right thing. → If only I **had said** the right thing.
- He wanted to sell his car before the crisis. → If only he **had sold** his car before the crisis.
- The children wanted to make a bigger effort for the exam. → If only the children **had made** a bigger effort for the exam.
- You didn't want to go back to university. → If only I **hadn't gone** back to university.

### Practice: regrets (*arrepentirse*)
- She regrets not spending more time with her children. → If only she **spent** more time with her children.
- Peter regrets not buying a house when they were cheap. → If only Peter **had bought** a house when they were cheap.
- Your boss regrets not dedicating more time to sales now. → If only my boss **dedicated** more time to sales now.
- My family regrets not moving to China three years ago. → If only my family **had moved** to China three years ago.
- The teacher regrets failing all her students last year. → If only the teacher **hadn't failed** all her students last year.

sections.title: 2. Three Common Acronyms
sections.content:
Pronounce each **letter** separately.

| Acronym | Stands for | Spanish | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **DIY** /ˌdiː aɪ ˈwaɪ/ | do it yourself | manualidades, bricolaje | *Are you good at DIYs?* |
| **AI** /ˌeɪ ˈaɪ/ | artificial intelligence | IA | *Are you scared of AI?* |
| **AKA** /ˌeɪ keɪ ˈeɪ/ | also known as | también conocido como | *Julia, AKA Jules* |

> ⚠ **AI**, not *IA*: the English order puts the **A first**. Repeat it many times until the order feels natural.

### Practice (Ask me…)
- Are you good at DIYs, and do you do them often? → Yes, I'm good at DIYs, but I don't do them often.
- Are you scared of AI? → For now, no, I'm not scared of AI.
- Is your name Julia, AKA Jules?

sections.title: 3. False Friend: Advice vs. Warning
sections.content:
- **advice** = *consejo* (uncountable: *a piece of advice*)
- **a warning** = *un aviso, una advertencia*

❌ *I got an advice saying four attempts left.*
✅ *I got a **warning** saying I had four attempts left.*

False friends appear when two languages evolve the same word in different directions. They're annoying, but you hear them so often that you end up remembering them.

title: English Time with Juls
topic: To Settle Down / Sports Equipment

sections.title: 1. Discussion: English as a Tool
sections.content:
A student asks: *Is it a good idea to set your phone to English?*

- It helps you stay **in touch with the language** through repetition, but it won't make a massive difference, because you're only reading.
- **Speak before you read.** Learning the spelling first creates bad pronunciation habits (*famous* pronounced as it's written).
- Better: **look up things you love in English.** Juls's example is caring for her plants: watching videos and googling in English, you learn *soil* (tierra), *to repot*, *leaves*… by **using** the words, not memorising them.
- Language is a **means** (*el medio*), not the objective, like walking: what matters is where you can go.
- Texting in English is useful because the phone **suggests words** you can start using.

### Vocabulary
| Word | Spanish |
|---|---|
| **soil** | tierra (de las plantas) |
| **to repot** | trasplantar a otra maceta |
| **to look after** | cuidar |
| **nothing is off limits** | no hay temas prohibidos |

sections.title: 2. Phrasal Verb: To Settle Down
sections.content:
**To settle down** has several related meanings:

| Meaning | Spanish | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Settle somewhere, establish yourself | establecerse, asentarse | *Is it easy to settle down and start a family?* |
| Lead a calmer, stable life | **sentar la cabeza** | *Do you think it's time for him to settle down?* |
| Calm down, stay still | calmarse, acomodarse | *We should wait for the audience to settle down.* |

⚠ **set up** is different: *montar algo*.

> **Formar una familia** → **start a family** (not *build/form a family*).

### Practice (Ask me…)
- Should we wait for the audience to settle down? → Yes, we should wait for the audience to settle down.
- Do you think it's time for him to settle down? → I think it's time for him to settle down.
- Is it easy to settle down and start a family?
- Did Susan settle down after she got married? → Yes, Susan settled down after she got married.
- Will they call the police if he doesn't settle down? → Yes, they will call the police if he doesn't settle down.

### Pronunciation: the *-ttle* sound (settle, little)
- **American option** (easier): the T becomes a soft flap, like a soft Spanish R: *se-rl*, *li-rl*.
- **British option**:
  1. The English **T has much more air** than the dry Spanish T.
  2. The English **L is rounder**: raise the back of the tongue, as if swallowing.
  3. The tongue **stays in the same position** from T to L: just release a puff of air for the T.
  4. To make it easier, slip a tiny, quick *e* between them: *set-e-l*.
- **Glottal stop** (*se'le*, *li'le*): very colloquial, used in some areas of England. Received Pronunciation (southern England) avoids it.
- **Exaggerate first**, then repeat a million times to build **muscle memory**.

sections.title: 3. Sports Equipment
sections.content:

| **a baseball bat** | un bate de béisbol | *bat* also means *murciélago*: *Baseball bats are usually made of wood.* |

sections.title: 1. Students' Questions: Feet First & Outdoor Activities
sections.content:
### *Estoy nadando con los pies por delante para no darme con las rocas*
→ **I'm swimming feet first so as not to hit the rocks.**
- **[body part] + first**: *feet first, head first* (*diving head first*), *hands first*.
- **so as not to / in order not to** = *para no*.
- Keep it simple: English is very practical.

> **Tip:** when you're at the beach or swimming, describe what you see and do **in English**. Even if you don't know the perfect way to say it, finding *a* way is great mental exercise.

### Outdoor & water activities

| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| **to keep your balance** | mantener el equilibrio |
| **canyoning** | barranquismo |
| **canoeing** | piragüismo |
| **rafting** | rafting |
| **rappelling** | rápel |
| **paddleboarding** | paddle surf |
| **crowded** | abarrotado, lleno de gente |

- *Are you able to keep your balance on a surfboard?* → Yes, for a few seconds, and then I fall.
- ⚠ For places, use **its**, not *his/her*: *Cádiz is known for **its** big waves.*

sections.title: 2. At the Doctor's: Blood Tests
sections.content:
English has no reflexive *hacerse*: if someone else does it to you, use **get**.

| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| hacerse un análisis de sangre | **to get a blood test** |
| sacarse sangre | **to get your blood drawn** *(draw/drew/drawn = also extraer, sacar)* |
| ir al médico | **to go to the doctor's** |
| el centro de salud | **the healthcare center** |

### Practice (Ask me…)
- Did you get a blood test this morning?
- Did you get your blood drawn this morning? → Yes, I got my blood drawn this morning.
- When was the last time you got a blood test?

### Other vocabulary from the conversation
- **needles** = agujas
- **faulty** = defectuoso: *Human beings are a little bit faulty.*
- **alive and kicking** = vivito y coleando
- **touch wood** = toco madera

title: English Time with Juls
topic: A 7-Day Trip (Compound Adjectives) / Get To Do

sections.title: 1. Number + Unit Adjectives: A Three-Week Holiday
sections.content:
*Unas vacaciones de tres semanas* is **not** *a holiday of three weeks*, but **a three-week holiday**.

### Why?
1. Join the **number + unit** with a **hyphen** (*dash*) → one word: *three-week*.
2. It becomes an **adjective**, so it goes **before the noun**.
3. Adjectives in English are **always singular** → *three-**week***, never *three-weeks*.

⚠ Classic mistake: ~~*a five stars hotel*~~ → **a five-star hotel**.

### Irregular plurals → use the singular form
- *people* → **person**: *a seven-**person** team*
- *children* → **child**: *a 20-**child** class*
- Watch the pronunciation: *pages* /ˈpeɪdʒɪz/ → *page* /peɪdʒ/: *a 500-page book*

### Practice
- Are you taking a three-week holiday? → Yes, I'm taking a **three-week holiday**.
- My boss is doing a course of seven months. → My boss is doing a **seven-month course**.
- I used to live in a house with four bedrooms. → I used to live in a **four-bedroom house**.
- She would like to stay in a hotel with five stars. → She would like to stay in a **five-star hotel**.
- My partner had a meeting of three hours today. → My partner had a **three-hour meeting** today.
- My boss is in charge of a team with seven people. → My boss is in charge of a **seven-person team**.
- There is a corridor with three meters in my office. → There is a **three-meter corridor** in my office.
- She teaches a class with 20 children on Fridays. → She teaches a **20-child class** on Fridays.
- I've never read a book with 500 pages before. → I've never read a **500-page book** before.
- We are excited to work in this program of two years. → We are excited to work in this **two-year program**.

> The long versions aren't technically wrong, but they sound unnatural. Start with durations (days, weeks, years) and build from there.

*program* (US) / *programme* (UK): both spellings are accepted, like *color/colour*.

sections.title: 2. Get To + Verb (Tener la oportunidad de)
sections.content:
**get to + verb** = *tener la oportunidad / la ocasión de hacer algo* (sometimes *conseguir*).

| | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **get to** + place | *llegar a*: *I get to the office at 9.* |
| **get to** + verb | *tener la oportunidad de*: *I **get to work** in something that I love.* |

It's a simpler, more natural alternative to *have the chance/opportunity to*.

> *Conseguir* sometimes works (*I got to finish my homework in time*), but not always: *consigo conocer a gente interesante en mi trabajo* sounds odd. The general meaning is **having the opportunity**.

### Practice (Ask me…)
- Did you get to enjoy your childhood without phones? → Yes, I got to enjoy my childhood without phones.
- Did your sister get to make friends in a summer camp? → Yes, my sister got to **make** friends in a summer camp. *(make friends, not "do friends")*
- Did you get to see your friends before they moved? → Yes, I got to see my friends before they moved.
- Do you get to meet great people at your job? → Yes, I get to meet great people at my job.
- Do actors get to watch the movie before it comes out?
- Do you usually get to say goodbye to everyone before you leave a party? → Not always.

### Bonus: an Irish exit
*Hacer bomba de humo / despedirse a la francesa* = **to do an Irish exit** (also a **French exit**): leaving a party quietly without saying goodbye.
- *I did an Irish exit because I didn't want to say goodbye to everyone.*
