title: English Time with Juls
topic: The Silent W + Dropping the T

sections.title: 1. Discussion: Juls's Classes & There Are No Silly Questions
sections.content:
The last class of the summer intensive week, and the last before the August break.

### The three weekly classes
| Class | Day | Focus |
|---|---|---|
| **English Time** | Monday | Intermediate to advanced content, with a mix of grammar, vocabulary, pronunciation… |
| **Essential English** | Wednesday | The **basis** of the language: frequent, fundamental concepts. Not necessarily *easier* |
| **Natural English** | Friday | Using the language like a native, not like an academic book |

### No hay preguntas tontas: there are no silly questions
Obsessing over levels (*I'm a B1…*) makes students afraid to ask "basic" questions, so their doubts never get solved and the mistakes stay. Ask, practise the solution, and the mistake goes away. A good teacher **never** judges.

### Vocabulary
| Expression | Spanish |
|---|---|
| **once in a blue moon** | de Pascuas a Ramos, muy de vuelta en cuando |
| **a geek** | un friki |
| **I could do it with my eyes closed** | lo podría hacer con los ojos cerrados |
| **a punching bag** | un saco de boxeo *(bag, not sack)* |

sections.title: 2. The Silent W (WR-)
sections.content:
When a word starts with **WR**, the **W is silent**: just pronounce the R.
- **writing** /ˈraɪtɪŋ/, not *"gwriting"* or *"ua-riting"*.
- It's much easier to pronounce this way!

| Word | Pronunciation | Spanish |
|---|---|---|
| **wrap** / **wrapping** | /ræp/ | envolver: *a chicken wrap*, *wrapping presents* |
| **wrist** | /rɪst/ | muñeca (la articulación) |
| **wrong** / **wrongly** | /rɒŋ/ | incorrecto / incorrectamente |
| **writer** | /ˈraɪtə/ | escritor/a |
| **wrestle** | /ˈresəl/ | forcejear, luchar (en plan juego) |
| **wrinkles** | /ˈrɪŋkəlz/ | arrugas |

**fight** vs. **wrestle**: *fight* = to fight for real; *wrestle* = to grapple or scuffle, more playful.

### Practice
- Are you good at **wrapping** presents?
- Have you ever broken your **wrist**? → No, I've never broken my wrist.
- Was the last answer **wrong**? → No, the last answer wasn't wrong.
- Would you like to be a **writer**?
- Did you use to **wrestle** with other children when you were younger?
- Do people usually spell your name **wrongly**?
- Are you getting **wrinkles** on your face?

### Face vocabulary
| English | Spanish |
|---|---|
| **crow's feet** | patas de gallo |
| **forehead lines** | arrugas de la frente |
| **smile lines** | líneas de expresión (de la sonrisa) |
| **bags under the eyes** / **dark circles** | bolsas / ojeras |

sections.title: 3. Dropping the T Between Words
sections.content:
Some words **do** pronounce the T on their own, but **drop it in connected speech** when the next word starts with a consonant, to avoid a cluster of consonants. (This is different from *listen*, where the T is *always* silent.)

| Written | Said |
|---|---|
| **next day** | *nex day* |
| **most people** | *mos people* |
| **just one** | *jus one* (in fast, colloquial speech, even before a vowel) |

Only the pronunciation changes, not the spelling. Say the words together, connected. Pronounce the T only if you want to stress the word strongly.

### Practice (make it negative)
- I have seven meetings next day. → I don't have seven meetings *nex(t) day*.
- Most people play an instrument. → *Mos(t) people* don't play an instrument.
- Just one person went to the cinema. → *Jus(t) one* person didn't go to the cinema.

To avoid a difficult cluster of consonants

title: English Time with Juls
topic: Adjectives with Over-

sections.title: 1. Discussion: Back to the Routine
sections.content:
The first class after the summer break. For Juls, **September feels more like the new year than January**.

- Some people get depressed in September; others feel new motivation. Juls is in the second team.
- **We have more power over how we feel than we think.** She decided to stop hating Sundays and the end of summer, and now she enjoys them.

### Schedule
Monday and Wednesday at **4:30** until 15 September; Friday (Natural English) at **2:00 PM**.

### Vocabulary
| Expression | Spanish |
|---|---|
| **back to reality / back to the routine** | vuelta a la realidad / a la rutina |
| **to resume (classes)** | retomar (las clases) |
| **bearable** | soportable |
| **to ramble** / **to beat around the bush** | enrollarse / irse por las ramas |
| **to mock / to imitate** | imitar (burlonamente) |
| **second nature** | algo natural, automático |

> Why speaking works better than writing: we remember songs after hearing them twice, but forget years of written study. The brain is built to learn language **orally**; writing came much later in evolution.

sections.title: 2. Adjectives with Over- (Sobre-)
sections.content:
**over-** = *sobre-*: it means **too much**, and many of these words have a direct Spanish equivalent. They are written as **one word**.

| Adjective | Meaning | Spanish |
|---|---|---|
| **overcrowded** | too many people in a place **at a specific moment** (concert, street, classroom) | abarrotado |
| **overpopulated** | too many **inhabitants** (city, country) | superpoblado |
| **overrated** | thought to be better than it really is | sobrevalorado *(to rate = valorar)* |
| **overloaded** | with too much content or load | sobrecargado *(to load = cargar)* |
| **overgrown** | (plants, garden) that has grown too much | sobrecrecido, descuidado *(grow → grown)* |
| **overestimated** | thought to be more capable than they really are | sobreestimado |

⚠ **Overwhelmed** is figurative (*sobrepasado*): *I'm overwhelmed with work.* **Overflowing** is only for liquids.

> **Tip:** these are long words, so pronounce every syllable and exaggerate the **intonation**, like a song: *o-ver-PO-pu-la-ted*. The melody helps you remember them.

### Practice (Ask me…)
- Will your garden be **overgrown** in three weeks?
- Was your boss **overestimated** by the CEO?
- Do most people think that *Titanic* is **overrated**? → I don't think so, its popularity is well-deserved.
- Which country is more **overpopulated**, India or Madagascar? → India, definitely.
- Was it **overcrowded** last time you went to a concert?

qs.q: A concert with far too many people at that moment is…
A country with too many inhabitants is…
A film everyone says is great, but really isn't, is…
A boat carrying too much merchandise is…
A garden where the plants have grown too much is…
'Me has sobreestimado.' →
'I'm ___ because I have too much work' (sobrepasado/a).
'Enrollarse / irse por las ramas' →
opts: to ramble / to beat around the bush
to rumble / to hit the bush
to roll / to go by the branches
qs.ans: to ramble / to beat around the bush

title: English Time with Juls
topic: Reported Speech

sections.title: 1. Reported Speech: The Logic
sections.content:
**Direct speech**: the exact words: *"I'm hungry," Pepito said.*
**Reported (indirect) speech**: we paraphrase the message: *Pepito said that he **was** hungry.*

It works **the same way as in Spanish**, so don't memorise tables: use your **logic**.

### Why the tense goes one step back
When you repeat what someone said, they said it **before now**, so the tense moves **one step back** on the timeline. Spanish does the same: *Pepito dijo que **tenía** hambre*, not *que tiene hambre*.

### Other automatic changes (perspective)
- **Possessives and pronouns**: *my brother* → *his brother*; *our holidays* → *their holidays*.
- **Time expressions**: *last week* → **the week before**; *at the moment* → **at that moment**.

### Tense changes seen in class
| Direct | Reported |
|---|---|
| present simple (*visit*) | past simple (*visited*) |
| present continuous (*am organizing*) | past continuous (*was organizing*) |
| past simple (*got fired*) | **past perfect** (*had got fired*), the past of the past = *pluscuamperfecto* |
| will | **would** + base verb (*would order*, never *would ordered*) |
| can | **could** |
| past perfect | stays the same (it can't go further back) |

> If the situation is still true, you *can* keep the present (*Kevin said his brother visits…*), but if you don't know, the past is the safe option.

### Is *that* optional?
Yes. *Peter said (that) he couldn't do it.* The two clauses have different subjects and work independently, so *that* is usually omitted.

sections.title: 2. Practice: Transform the Sentences
sections.content:
| Direct speech | Reported speech |
|---|---|
| "I'm hungry," Pepito said. | Pepito said that he **was** hungry. |
| "My brother visits his girlfriend every year," Kevin said. | Kevin said that **his** brother **visited** **his** girlfriend every year. |
| "I got fired last week," Peter said. | Peter said that he **had got fired** **the week before**. |
| "We went surfing on our last holidays," my parents said. | My parents said that they **had gone** surfing on **their** last holidays. |
| "I am organizing a launch party," my boss said. | My boss said that he **was organizing** a launch party. |
| "We work out three times a week," my friends said. | My friends said that they **worked out** three times a week. |
| "I found out the answer," Susan said. | Susan said that she **had found out** the answer. |
| "We will order three machines," my colleague said. | My colleague said that they **would order** three machines. |
| "I can't do it," Peter said. | Peter said that he **couldn't** do it. |
| "I broke up with my boyfriend," Lucy said. | Lucy said that she **had broken up** with **her** boyfriend. |
| "We won't do it," the policeman said. | The policeman said that they **wouldn't** do it. |
| "My mom is dealing with something at the moment," John said. | John said that **his** mom **was dealing** with something **at that moment**. |

### Notes
- ⚠ *had got fired*, not *had been got fired*: **get** already works as the passive auxiliary.
- ⚠ **order** is a false friend: it means *pedir* (food, products), not *ordenar*.
- **to deal with** someone/something = *lidiar con* alguien/algo.

> **Practice idea:** tell a story out loud about your day: *My boss said that he was going to go to the zoo, but in the end he didn't go. Then he said that he would call me, but he never did.*

qs.ans: Pepito said that he was hungry.

qs.ans: My boss said that he was organizing a launch party.

title: English Time with Juls
topic: Instead Of

sections.title: 1. Discussion: New Schedule & Juls's Master's Degree
sections.content:
### New schedule
Monday and Wednesday classes are now at **5:00 PM** (half an hour earlier than before the summer); Friday stays at **2:00 PM**. Juls has started a **master's degree in teacher training**.

### Her view on education
- She studied **English philology** and has taught since she was 15–16; she enjoys teaching more now than when she started.
- Learning is in our nature: children ask *why* all the time. Rigid, overly serious schooling **kills curiosity**, which creates a **vicious circle**, because teachers are trained the same way they were taught.
- **You don't learn faster by taking it seriously.** The brain absorbs more when it's enjoying itself: *learning through playing*.

### Vocabulary
| Expression | Spanish |
|---|---|
| **Would you mind telling us…?** | ¿Te importaría contarnos…? *(mind + -ing)* |
| **a master's degree** | un máster |
| **teacher training** | formación del profesorado |
| **obsolete** | obsoleto/a |
| **bland** | soso/a, insulso/a |
| **to kill curiosity** | matar la curiosidad |
| **a vicious circle** | un círculo vicioso |
| **experience is the best teacher** | la experiencia es la mejor maestra |

sections.title: 2. Instead Of (En vez de / En lugar de)
sections.content:
**instead of** = *en vez de, en lugar de* (⚠ *of* has only one F).

| After *instead of* | Example |
|---|---|
| **noun / name** | *My sister went to Australia last year instead of **New Zealand**.* |
| **verb → -ING** | ***Instead of traveling** so much, you should save money.* |
| **object pronoun** | *She should marry me instead of **him**.* |

### Why -ING?
**Rule of thumb** (*la regla de oro*): after a **preposition**, a verb always takes **-ing** (the gerund). Spanish uses the infinitive (*en vez de **ir***), English uses the gerund (*instead of **going***).

### Practice: build the sentence
- **Instead of traveling** so much, you should save money.
- **Instead of trying** an impossible diet, you should exercise more / do more exercise.
- My sister went to Australia last year **instead of** New Zealand.
- She should marry me **instead of him**.
- **Instead of complaining** so much, you should do something about it.
- I will call her tomorrow **instead of them**.

### Translations
- *En lugar de culpar a alguien, él debería aceptar su error.* → **Instead of blaming** someone, he should accept his mistake.
- *En vez del lunes, ¿por qué no tenemos la clase el martes?* → **Instead of Monday**, why don't we have the class on Tuesday?
- *Él debería contármelo a mí en lugar de a él.* → He should **tell me** instead of **him**.
- *¿No preferirías viajar al pasado en vez de al futuro?* → Wouldn't you prefer to travel to the past **instead of** the future?
- *En vez de ahorrar, ¿por qué no inviertes?* → **Instead of saving**, why don't you invest?

### *Tell me*, not *tell me it*
With **tell**, the message is implied, so there's no need for *it*: *contármelo* → **tell me**. Add an object only to be specific: *tell me the truth / a secret*.

title: English Time with Juls
topic: Easily + Superlatives

sections.title: 1. Discussion: Learning a Second Language
sections.content:
- **Everyone has already learned a language**: your first one. A second language isn't like learning to drive or play an instrument for the first time, so we should **mimic** the way we learned our first language.
- A wise colleague (a retired university teacher with a PhD in education and AI) told Juls: *"You never stop being a student. The moment you stop learning, you stop developing as a teacher."*
- When students aren't progressing, it isn't always their fault: teachers should be **humble**, not *preachers*.

### Vocabulary
| Expression | Spanish |
|---|---|
| **stubborn** | cabezota, terco/a |
| **humble** | humilde |
| **to mimic** | imitar |
| **my last days in my 20s** | mis últimos días con veintitantos |
| **I feel like an impostor** | me siento un/a impostor/a |
| **to know something by heart** | saberse algo de memoria |
| **fingers crossed / touch wood** | crucemos los dedos / toco madera |

Astronomical autumn starts around **22–23 September**; meteorological autumn starts on **1 September**.

sections.title: 2. Superlatives Review
sections.content:
| Adjective | Superlative | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **One syllable** | **the + -est** | big → the biggest, small → the smallest, fast → the fastest, short → the shortest |
| **Two or more syllables** | **the most** + adjective | popular → the most popular, beautiful → the most beautiful |
| ⚠ **Two syllables ending in -Y** | **the + -iest** (exception) | happy → the happiest, funny → the funniest, easy → the easiest, early → the earliest |
| **Irregular** | change completely | good → better → the best; bad → worse → the worst; far → further → the furthest |

❌ *the most happy*, *more happy* → ✅ **the happiest**, **happier**.

sections.title: 3. Easily + Superlative
sections.content:
**easily** (adverb) + superlative = *fácilmente*: it's **clearly / obviously** number one. Another way to say **by far**.
- Position: **between the verb and the superlative**, just like in Spanish.
- *El fútbol es **fácilmente** el deporte más popular en España.* → *Football is **easily the most popular** sport in Spain.*
- *This is **by far** the best class I've attended.*

### Practice
- Ferrari / popular Italian car → Ferrari is **easily the most popular** Italian car.
- Michael Jordan / good basketball player → Michael Jordan is **easily the best** basketball player.
- Coca-Cola / consumed soft drink → Coca-Cola is **easily the most consumed** soft drink.
- Madrid / beautiful city in Europe → Madrid is **easily the most beautiful** city in Europe.
- The discovery of penicillin / big discovery in history → The discovery of penicillin is **easily the biggest** discovery **in** history.
- Jeff Bezos / rich man in the world → Jeff Bezos is **easily the richest** man in the world.
- *Game of Thrones* / great TV show → *Game of Thrones* is **easily the greatest** TV show.

### Translations
- *Esta es fácilmente la persona más pequeña que he visto.* → This is easily **the smallest / tiniest / shortest** person I have (ever) seen.
- *Ese fue, fácilmente, el momento más feliz de mi vida.* → That was easily **the happiest** moment of my life.

### Refresco
- **soft drink** (general), **fizzy drink** (British), **soda** (American). Choose one!
- For water: **sparkling water**, not *fizzy water*.

qs.q: Where does 'easily' go in a superlative sentence?

qs.ans: Between the verb and the superlative

title: English Time with Juls
topic: To Sound + New Adjectives

sections.title: 1. That Sounds + Adjective
sections.content:
Just like Spanish *sonar* used figuratively (*suena bien, suena interesante*), English uses **sound** + **adjective**:

> **(That) + noun + sound(s) + adjective**: *That sounds good.* / *That trip sounds lovely.*

- Remember the **-s** in the third person: *That **sounds**…*
- Start with **that** to make it a natural **reaction** to something someone just told you.
- Only a single **adjective** fits after *sounds*: ❌ *That solution sounds a wild idea* → ✅ *That solution sounds **wild***.
- ⚠ **ring** = *sonar* for a phone, alarm or doorbell; **sound** is the general verb. (*It rings a bell* = me suena.)

### Practice
| Spanish | English |
|---|---|
| Ese tema suena confuso. | That **topic** sounds **confusing**. |
| Esa actuación suena horrorosa. | That **performance** sounds **awful**. |
| Ese viaje suena adorable. | That **trip** sounds **lovely**. |
| Esa historia suena sosa. | That **story** sounds **bland**. |
| Esa opinión suena infundada. | That **opinion** sounds **unfounded**. |
| Esa lesión suena grave. | That **injury** sounds **serious**. |
| Ese procedimiento suena arriesgado. | That **procedure** sounds **risky**. |
| Esa solución suena descabellada. | That **solution** sounds **far-fetched**. |
| Esa excusa suena inventada. | That **excuse** sounds **made up**. |
| Esa conversación suena controvertida. | That **conversation** sounds **controversial**. |
| Ese invento suena innovador. | That **invention** sounds **innovative**. |
| Esa ciudad suena deprimente/gris. | That **city** sounds **dreary**. |
| Ese pueblo suena pintoresco. | That **village** sounds **picturesque**. |

sections.title: 2. Notes on the New Adjectives
sections.content:
- **awful** /ˈɔːfəl/: a great alternative to *terrible/horrible*. Long, closed *o* plus a weak *-ful*.
- ⚠ **terrific** = **great, fantastic** (positive!), not *terrible*.
- ⚠ **terrified** = how you **feel** (*aterrorizado/a*), not a description of a thing.
- **lovely**: very British, used for everything nice: *Oh, lovely! That's lovely.*
- ⚠ **bland** = **soso/a** (false friend, not *blando*): *The food is bland.*
- **story** (a tale, a narrative) vs. **history** (past events): *the history of humanity*, *the story of my life*.
- **topic** = a general subject (*tema*); **issue** = a more specific matter (*asunto*).
- **serious** = *grave*. *Grave* exists, but it sounds excessive (and also means *tumba*).
- **procedure** /prəˈsiːdʒə/: three syllables, stress on *-ce-*, with a voiced *dʒ* at the end.
- **far-fetched** = *descabellado/a, rebuscado/a* (*fetch* = ir a buscar y traer, as in *play fetch* with a dog). Pronounce *-tched* /tʃt/.
- **made up** = *inventado/a* (from the phrasal verb **make up**). Latin vs. Anglo-Saxon: *invented* is correct but sounds academic, so prefer the Anglo-Saxon / phrasal verb option.
- **trip** (noun) vs. **travel** (verb). *Travels* as a noun is poetic or literary (*Travels with My Aunt*).
- **invention** (not *invent*) and **innovative** (not *innovator*): watch the endings!
- **dreary** = grey, gloomy **and** depressing, ideal for describing a place. (**gloomy** = sombrío, nublado.)
- **picturesque** /ˌpɪktʃəˈresk/ = *pintoresco*, from *picture*.
